I am not making a Luddite argument. I am not suggesting that difficulty is inherently virtuous or that we should preserve friction for its own sake. Albert Borgmann drew a useful distinction between what he called "devices" and "focal things"—a central heating system is a device that delivers warmth without engagement, while a wood-burning fireplace is a focal thing that organizes a set of practices (splitting wood, tending fire, gathering around the hearth) that connect people to the physical world and to each other. Borgmann did not argue that we should abandon central heating. He argued that a life composed entirely of device-mediated experiences is impoverished in ways that are difficult to articulate but easy to feel. I think he was right, and I think the distinction has only grown more urgent. We need a more sophisticated framework for evaluating technological adoption than the simple question "Does this make things easier?" Sometimes the answer is yes, and the result is liberation. Sometimes the answer is yes, and the result is the atrophying of a capacity we didn't realize we valued until it was gone.

## Flourishing in the Age of AI

These questions acquire new urgency with the emergence of artificial intelligence. We are entering an era in which machines can perform not just physical labor but cognitive labor—writing, analysis, design, even forms of creativity—at a level that matches or exceeds average human performance. This raises a question that previous waves of technology only hinted at: What is the human being *for*?

The optimistic vision deserves to be taken seriously on its strongest terms. It is not merely that AI will free us from drudgery, though it may. The deeper promise is democratization. A student in rural Kenya with access to a sophisticated AI tutor could develop capacities that no previous generation could have accessed regardless of talent. An artist without formal training could use AI tools to compress the feedback loops that accelerate learning, reaching in months a level of competence that once required years of institutional access. AI could make the conditions for Aristotelian excellence—education, mentorship, exposure to great work—available to millions who have been excluded from them by accident of geography or class. This is a serious argument, and anyone concerned with human flourishing must grapple with it honestly.

But the historical record urges caution about the automatic conversion of capability into flourishing. The washing machine freed hours of domestic labor. Some of those hours were redirected toward education and civic engagement. Many were absorbed by rising standards of cleanliness and by television. There is no automatic mechanism by which saved time or expanded access converts into the development of human excellence. That conversion requires intention, cultural infrastructure, and a shared understanding of what a good life looks like—precisely the things a culture obsessed with technological capability tends to neglect.

The deeper challenge of AI, however, is not economic but existential, and it centers on a psychological claim I want to develop carefully: human motivation is deeply entangled with the sense that one's efforts matter—that the struggle to articulate an idea or master a skill produces something that would not otherwise exist.

The obvious counterexample is that people still run marathons even though cars exist. People still knit even though factories produce sweaters. This suggests that process-satisfaction can survive the obsolescence of output. And for some activities, in some contexts, I think that is true. But running and knitting persist partly because they have been *reframed*—they are understood as exercises in personal challenge, as practices valued for what they cultivate in the practitioner. That reframing took decades and required cultural work. It did not happen automatically.

Now consider what happens when AI can produce competent novels, compose moving music, or generate scientific hypotheses. The marathon analogy breaks down in an important way: running was never primarily an instrumental activity for most people, but writing, composing, and researching often are. They are activities in which the human practitioner's sense of purpose is bound up with the belief that their cognitive struggle produces something of value—something that could not exist without them. When a machine can produce comparable output instantaneously, that belief is threatened. Not destroyed, perhaps, but eroded. And motivation, deprived of the oxygen of perceived significance, tends to quietly suffocate.

This is the most underexplored dimension of the AI question. We focus on economics—who will lose their jobs—and on ethics—how to prevent misuse. But the motivational question may matter more for human flourishing than either. A world in which people *can* create but increasingly feel that their creations are redundant is not a world that Aristotle would recognize as conducive to *eudaimonia*.

## Toward a More Deliberate Relationship

What would it look like to take this seriously—not as abstract philosophy but as a practical orientation?

Consider the case of a school deciding whether to integrate AI writing tools into its curriculum. The efficiency argument is straightforward: students can produce better drafts faster, freeing time for higher-order thinking. But a school that has thought carefully about flourishing might ask different questions. It might recognize that the struggle to organize one's thoughts in prose—the halting, frustrating, recursive process of writing—is not an obstacle to learning but a primary mechanism of it. It might adopt AI tools for certain purposes (research assistance, grammar checking) while deliberately preserving the friction of composition for others. It might, in other words, make a *discriminating* choice rather than a wholesale adoption.

This is what deliberate relationship with technology looks like in practice: not rejection, not uncritical embrace, but the cultivation of judgment about which frictions are merely inconvenient and which are constitutive of the experiences we value. A family might make similar discriminations—using GPS on highways but navigating by map on vacation, not out of nostalgia but out of a considered understanding that wayfinding cultivates spatial awareness, attentiveness, and the possibility of surprise. A company might resist automating its mentorship processes even when AI could deliver more "efficient" feedback, recognizing that the relationship between mentor and apprentice is not a delivery mechanism for information but a formative human bond.

These are small examples, and I do not pretend they are adequate to the scale of the challenge. The forces driving technological adoption—competitive pressure, profit motive, the sheer momentum of convenience—are enormous, and individual deliberation alone cannot redirect them. But the cultural conversation has to begin somewhere, and it begins with the recognition that we are not merely consumers of technology but human beings shaped by it, capable of asking what kind of shaping we will accept.

We have built a civilization of astonishing capability. We can edit genes, communicate instantaneously across the globe, and train machines to mimic the patterns of human thought. What we have not yet built is a wisdom adequate to these capabilities—a shared framework for deciding which powers to exercise, which to restrain, and how to preserve the conditions under which human beings can develop the excellences that make life worth living. Thinkers from Postman to Borgmann to Turkle have been pointing toward this gap for decades. The gap has only widened.

That framework will not emerge from technology itself. It will emerge, if it emerges at all, from the oldest and least efficient of human activities: careful thought, honest conversation, and the slow, difficult work of deciding together what kind of life is worth living. In an age that prizes speed above almost everything, this may be the most countercultural act available to us—and the most necessary.

# The Paradox of Capacity: Technology, Trade-offs, and What It Means to Flourish

In 2023, researchers at the University of Chicago published a study in which participants were offered money to deactivate their Facebook accounts for four weeks. Those who accepted reported measurable increases in subjective well-being, more time spent with friends and family, and reduced political polarization—but also said they felt less informed and more socially disconnected. When the experiment ended, most reactivated their accounts. Here, compressed into a single finding, is the essential puzzle of modern technology: a tool that simultaneously enriches and diminishes life, that we recognize as costly yet choose to retain, and whose trade-offs resist any simple accounting.

This puzzle points toward a question our civilization has been remarkably reluctant to examine with rigor: Does the relentless expansion of technological capability actually make human lives go well?

The default assumption of modernity is that it does. We treat technological progress as roughly synonymous with human progress, and we have centuries of compelling evidence to support the conflation. Vaccines, sanitation, refrigeration, anesthesia—these are not trivial gains. They represent the elimination of suffering on a scale that would have seemed miraculous to our ancestors. Global life expectancy has more than doubled since 1900. Child mortality has fallen by over 90 percent. Anyone tempted to romanticize pre-technological life should spend an afternoon reading accounts of pre-modern dentistry or childbirth. The case for technology as a force for human flourishing begins with the body, and at the level of the body, it is overwhelming.

But flourishing is not merely the absence of suffering, just as health is not merely the absence of disease. Aristotle's concept of *eudaimonia*—often translated as "flourishing" or "living well"—encompassed not just material security but the active exercise of distinctly human capacities: practical wisdom, the ability to deliberate and choose well; deep friendship built through sustained mutual attention; the pursuit of craft and mastery; the capacity to perceive and create beauty; and meaningful participation in civic life. These are not luxuries appended to survival. They are, on this account, what survival is *for*. And it is precisely here—in the space between solving problems and living well—that the relationship between technology and human flourishing becomes genuinely complicated.

## The Instrumentalist Illusion

We tend to think of technologies as neutral instruments. A hammer can build a house or break a window; the moral weight belongs to the user, not the tool. This framework feels intuitive, and it is largely wrong. Technologies are not neutral. They carry within them assumptions about what matters, what deserves attention, and how time should be spent. They restructure incentives, reshape habits, and gradually remodel the inner landscape of the people who use them.

Consider the smartphone. Described instrumentally, it is a device that enables communication, provides access to information, and facilitates navigation. Described honestly, it is a technology that has fundamentally altered the texture of daily consciousness for billions of people. A 2022 review published in *Nature Human Behaviour* found that the average person touches their phone over 2,600 times per day and that heavy smartphone use is associated with reduced capacity for sustained attention, diminished working memory, and increased anxiety. The technology has compressed the space between stimulus and response. It has made solitude functionally difficult. It has created an attentional environment in which the human mind is perpetually solicited, perpetually interrupted, perpetually offered an escape from whatever is immediately present.

None of this was the explicit intention of the smartphone's designers. It is simply what the technology does by virtue of what it is—a portal to an infinite feed of variable rewards, carried in the pocket, available at every moment. The philosopher of technology Langdon Winner argued decades ago that artifacts have politics. They also have psychologies. They shape the felt quality of experience whether we intend them to or not.

This does not mean the smartphone is a net negative. It means that adopting it involved a trade-off that most of us never consciously made. We gained extraordinary convenience and connectivity. We lost something harder to name—a certain quality of presence, an ease with stillness, a capacity for sustained attention that previous generations could take for granted. The trade-off may well be worth it. But it was a trade-off, and we should be honest about that.

## The Efficiency Trap

Modern technology is, above all, a project of optimization. It seeks to make processes faster, cheaper, more convenient, more frictionless. And optimization is genuinely valuable—right up to the point where it begins to erode the very things that make life meaningful.

Many of the experiences central to human flourishing are inherently inefficient. Learning a musical instrument is inefficient. Maintaining a deep friendship requires an extravagant expenditure of time that could be "better" spent. Raising children is, by any rational metric, a catastrophically poor allocation of resources. The things that constitute a rich human life—craft, relationship, contemplation, struggle, physical engagement with the material world—are almost universally slow, difficult, and resistant to optimization.

When technology optimizes away friction indiscriminately, it risks optimizing away meaning. The GPS that removes the possibility of getting lost also removes the possibility of the unexpected encounter. The AI that generates a competent essay in seconds also removes the laborious process of thinking through a problem in prose—a process that, for the writer, is not merely a means to an end but a mode of understanding.

I want to be careful here. I am not making a Luddite argument. I am not suggesting that difficulty is inherently virtuous or that we should preserve friction for its own sake. I am suggesting that we need a more sophisticated framework for evaluating technological adoption than the simple question "Does this make things easier?" Sometimes the answer is yes, and the result is genuine human benefit—no one mourns the hand-wringing of laundry. Sometimes the answer is yes, and the result is the quiet atrophying of a capacity we didn't realize we valued until it was gone.

## Flourishing in the Age of AI

These questions acquire new urgency with the emergence of artificial intelligence. We are entering an era in which machines can perform not just physical labor but cognitive labor—writing, analysis, design, even forms of creativity—at a level that matches or exceeds average human performance. This raises a question that previous waves of technology only hinted at: What is the human being *for*?

It is worth distinguishing between different dimensions of this challenge. The economic dimension—technological unemployment, the displacement of workers by automation—is serious and demands serious policy responses, from revised education systems to new models of income distribution. But I want to focus on a challenge that is less discussed and potentially more profound: the existential one.

The optimistic vision of AI is one of liberation and democratization. If AI handles routine cognitive drudgery, humans are freed for higher-order activities—creative expression, philosophical inquiry, the cultivation of wisdom. Moreover, AI tools might genuinely *expand* access to creative expression: a person with a musical idea but no formal training can now realize it; a small business owner can produce professional-quality design work; a scientist can explore hypotheses at a pace previously impossible. These are real gains, and they deserve to be taken seriously. AI as collaborator—as a tool that amplifies human creativity rather than replacing it—is not merely a comforting fantasy. It is one genuinely possible future.

But the historical record counsels caution about the "liberation" narrative. The washing machine genuinely freed up hours of domestic labor. Some of those hours were redirected toward education and civic engagement. But American time-use surveys show that much of the time saved by household technologies was absorbed by rising standards of cleanliness, expanded consumption, and, eventually, television—which by the 1970s consumed an average of six hours per household per day. There is no automatic mechanism by which saved time converts into flourishing. That conversion requires intention, cultural infrastructure, and a shared understanding of what a good life looks like—precisely the things a culture obsessed with capability tends to neglect.

The deeper existential challenge is this: if a machine can write a serviceable novel, compose a beautiful piece of music, or solve a scientific problem, what happens to the human motivation to attempt these things? The standard response is that humans will still value the *process* of creation, independent of the output. I believe this is partly true and partly wishful. Human motivation is complex, and it is deeply entangled with the sense that one's efforts matter—that the struggle to articulate an idea or master a skill produces something that would not otherwise exist. When that sense is undermined, motivation tends to follow. We do not see many people passionately training to perform arithmetic by hand.

The most promising path lies in neither uncritical embrace nor reflexive resistance, but in what we might call *deliberate complementarity*: structuring our use of AI so that it handles what humans find genuinely tedious while preserving the domains where struggle, mastery, and personal expression constitute the point. The musician who uses AI to handle mixing and arrangement while composing melodies by hand; the scientist who uses AI to survey literature while formulating hypotheses through her own thinking; the writer who uses AI to check facts while insisting on finding her own sentences—these represent a relationship with technology that enhances rather than hollows out human agency.

## Toward a More Deliberate Relationship

What would it look like to take the relationship between technology and flourishing seriously—not just philosophically, but practically?

It would begin with the recognition that technological adoption is not inevitable in the way we often pretend it is. We make choices about which technologies to embrace, how deeply to integrate them, and what boundaries to maintain. And there are models for doing this well. The Amish, often caricatured as technophobes, actually employ a sophisticated communal evaluation process: new technologies are tested by selected families and adopted only if they strengthen community bonds and family life. Cal Newport's "digital minimalism" movement has helped thousands of people restructure their relationship with technology around intentionally chosen values rather than default settings. These are not anti-technology positions. They are *pro-deliberation* positions.

Three principles might guide a more thoughtful approach. First, *the displacement question*: before adopting a technology, ask not only what it enables but what it displaces. What capacity might atrophy? What quality of experience might be foreclosed? Second, *the autonomy test*: does this technology expand my genuine options, or does it create new compulsions disguised as conveniences? Third, *the depth criterion*: does this technology support or undermine the conditions for deep attention, sustained relationship, and meaningful work—the foundations of *eudaimonia*?

These are not questions that technology can answer for us. They require the oldest and least efficient of human activities: careful thought, honest conversation, and the slow, difficult work of deciding—individually and collectively—what kind of life is worth living.

We have built a civilization of astonishing capability. We can edit genes, communicate instantaneously across the globe, and train machines to mimic the patterns of human thought. What we have not yet built is a wisdom adequate to these capabilities—a shared framework for deciding which powers to exercise, which to restrain, and how to preserve the conditions under which human beings can genuinely thrive. Building that framework is not a technical problem. It is, in the deepest sense, a human one. And it may be the most important work we can do.

Anyone tempted to romanticize pre-technological life should spend an afternoon reading accounts of pre-modern dentistry or childbirth. The case for technology as a force for human flourishing begins with the body, and at the level of the body, it is overwhelming.

But flourishing is not merely the absence of suffering, just as health is not merely the absence of disease. To make sense of the difference, we need a conception of what flourishing actually involves—and for that, I want to draw on a framework that is old enough to predate every technology under discussion. The Aristotelian concept of *eudaimonia* holds that a good human life consists not in the accumulation of pleasure or capability but in the development and exercise of distinctly human excellences: practical wisdom, courage, the capacity for deep friendship, the ability to perceive and create beauty, the sustained exercise of judgment under conditions of genuine uncertainty. These excellences require certain material conditions—conditions technology can provide. But they also require struggle, embodied engagement, and the kind of sustained attention that functions as a precondition for almost everything else on the list.

Why Aristotle rather than, say, a utilitarian calculus that simply aggregates well-being and likely comes down on the side of technological adoption? Because utilitarianism struggles to account for the *qualitative* dimensions of experience that most people, on reflection, care about deeply. A life of frictionless consumption that maximizes momentary satisfaction scores well on utilitarian metrics while failing to capture what most of us actually mean when we say a life has gone well. The Aristotelian framework takes seriously the possibility that some forms of difficulty are constitutive of flourishing rather than obstacles to it. This distinction turns out to matter enormously when evaluating technology.

## The Architecture of Attention

We tend to think of technologies as neutral instruments. A hammer can build a house or break a window; the moral weight belongs to the user, not the tool. Described honestly, it is a technology that has fundamentally altered the texture of daily consciousness for billions of people. I should note that the empirical literature on this point is more contested than popular discourse suggests—the debates around Jonathan Haidt's work and the replication difficulties in screen-time research are real, and confident causal claims deserve scrutiny. But even the more cautious readings of the evidence support a modest version of the claim: a portal to an infinite feed of variable rewards, carried in the pocket, available at every moment, changes something about the structure of attention. It compresses the space between stimulus and response. It makes solitude functionally difficult. It creates an attentional environment in which the mind is perpetually solicited.

None of this was the explicit intention of the smartphone's designers. It is simply what the technology does by virtue of what it is—and by virtue of the business models that govern its content ecosystem. We gained extraordinary convenience and connectivity. We lost something harder to name—a certain quality of presence, an ease with stillness, a capacity for the kind of sustained attention that the Aristotelian excellences specifically require. The trade-off may well be worth it. But it was a trade-off, and we should be honest about that.

The things that constitute a rich human life—craft, relationship, contemplation, physical engagement with the material world—are almost universally slow, difficult, and resistant to optimization.

The AI that generates a competent essay in seconds also removes the laborious process of thinking through a problem in prose—a process that, for the writer, is not merely a means to an end but a mode of understanding.

I want to be careful here, but not so careful that I say nothing. I am not suggesting that difficulty is inherently virtuous. I am arguing, specifically, that the *kinds* of difficulty involved in developing human excellences—the struggle to master a skill, to sustain attention, to understand another person—are not obstacles to flourishing but *part of its substance*. A framework that treats all friction as a problem to be solved will inevitably erode the conditions under which these excellences develop.

And I need to acknowledge a tension in this argument: the luxury of treating friction as meaningful is unevenly distributed. For a person working two jobs, the food delivery app is not eliminating a "sensory ritual"—it is saving scarce time that might go toward sleep, or a child's homework. The deliberate embrace of difficulty presupposes a baseline of material security that billions of people lack. Any serious framework for evaluating technology must grapple with this: the same tool that impoverishes experience for the affluent may be genuinely liberating for the precarious. The class dimension of technological adoption is not a footnote; it is central to any honest analysis.

## Flourishing in the Age of AI

These questions acquire new urgency with artificial intelligence. We are entering an era in which machines can perform not just physical labor but cognitive labor—writing, analysis, design, even forms of creativity—at a level that matches or exceeds average human performance. This raises a question that previous waves of technology only hinted at: What is the human being *for*?

A serious techno-optimist would respond that this question has been asked before and has always answered itself. People mourned the loss of oral memory after writing, navigational skill after maps, mental arithmetic after calculators. In every case, humanity adapted and found new forms of meaning. Why should this moment be different?

I think there are three reasons, and they are worth stating plainly. First, the *pace* of change: previous technological transitions unfolded over generations, allowing cultural adaptation; AI capabilities are advancing on timescales of months. Second, the *scope*: we are not displacing a single cognitive skill but potentially the entire category of cognitive labor, which is where most people in developed economies derive both livelihood and identity. Third, the *design incentives*: these technologies are being developed primarily within commercial frameworks optimized for engagement and profit, not for human development. Any one of these factors would warrant caution. Together, they constitute something genuinely unprecedented.

The optimistic vision is one of liberation. If AI handles routine cognitive work, humans will be freed to pursue creative expression, philosophical inquiry, deep relationship. This is essentially the same promise made about earlier labor-saving technologies, and the historical record is instructive. The washing machine genuinely freed hours of domestic labor. Some of those hours were redirected toward education and civic engagement. But liberated time has a persistent tendency to be captured—by new forms of work, by consumption, by entertainment designed to monetize attention. There is no automatic mechanism by which saved time converts into flourishing. That conversion requires intention, cultural infrastructure, and a shared understanding of what a good life looks like—precisely the things a culture obsessed with capability tends to neglect.

The deeper challenge is existential. If a machine can write a serviceable novel, compose a beautiful piece of music, or solve a scientific problem, what happens to the human motivation to attempt these things? The standard response is that humans will still value the *process* of creation, independent of the output. I believe this is partly true and partly wishful. Human motivation is deeply entangled with the sense that one's efforts matter—that the struggle to articulate an idea or master a skill produces something that would not otherwise exist. When that sense is undermined, motivation tends to follow. This is not speculation; it is visible already in the demoralization reported by illustrators, translators, and junior writers who find their skills suddenly commoditized. The Aristotelian excellence of *craft*—the deep satisfaction of hard-won mastery—depends on a world in which mastery means something. We are building a world that may inadvertently tell millions of people that it doesn't.

## Toward a More Deliberate Relationship

What would it look like to take this seriously—not as abstract philosophy but as a guide for actual decisions?

Consider a concrete case. In 2023, several school districts faced the question of whether to integrate AI writing tools into their curricula. The easy path was full adoption: students would learn to use AI as a productivity tool, preparing them for the workplace. Some districts chose a different path. They permitted AI for research and brainstorming but required that all formal writing be composed without it, on the grounds that the struggle to organize one's thoughts in prose is itself a form of cognitive development—not a problem to be optimized away but a capacity to be cultivated. This is what a deliberate relationship with technology looks like in practice: not rejection, but a conscious decision about which frictions to preserve and why, grounded in a substantive vision of what education is for.

The same logic extends beyond schools. Ivan Illich's concept of "convivial tools"—technologies that enhance human capability without degrading human autonomy—offers a useful test. A bicycle is convivial: it extends what the body can do while remaining fully under the rider's control. An algorithmic feed is not: it extends access to information while systematically eroding the user's capacity for self-directed attention. The question is not whether a technology is powerful but whether it leaves the user more capable or more dependent.

This framework demands that we ask, before each major adoption, not just "What does this enable?" but "What does this displace? What capacity does this allow to wither? What quality of experience does this foreclose?" And—crucially—"Who bears the costs, and who reaps the benefits?" These are not rhetorical questions. They are questions that institutions, communities, and individuals can actually answer, if they are willing to treat convenience as one value among many rather than the supreme value before which all others yield.

We have built a civilization of astonishing capability. We can edit genes, communicate instantaneously across the globe, and train machines to mimic the patterns of human thought. What we have not yet built is a wisdom adequate to these capabilities—a shared framework for deciding which powers to exercise, which to restrain, and how to preserve the conditions under which human beings can genuinely thrive.

That framework will not emerge from technology itself. It will require the oldest and least efficient of human activities: careful thought, honest conversation, and the slow work of deciding together what kind of life is worth living. Whether we are actually capable of that slowness, in a culture that has spent decades engineering it away, is a question I cannot answer with confidence. It may be the most important question we face.

Sometimes the answer is yes, and the result is the quiet atrophying of a capacity we didn't realize we valued until it was gone.

## Flourishing in the Age of AI

These questions acquire a new urgency with the emergence of artificial intelligence and automation. We are entering an era in which machines can perform not just physical labor but cognitive labor—writing, analysis, design, even forms of creativity—at a level that matches or exceeds average human performance. This raises a question that previous waves of technology only hinted at: What is the human being *for*?

The optimistic vision is one of liberation. This is essentially the same promise that was made about earlier labor-saving technologies, and it has occasionally been fulfilled. The washing machine genuinely did free up hours of domestic labor. Some of those hours were redirected toward education, civic engagement, and personal development.

But the historical record also shows that liberated time has a tendency to be captured—and the mechanisms of capture have grown more sophisticated with each technological generation. Some of this recapture is economic: new technologies raise the baseline of expected productivity, creating pressure to work more simply to maintain one's position. Some of it is cultural: the attention economy has become extraordinarily adept at engineering the absorption of unstructured time, deploying algorithmic precision to convert idle moments into monetizable engagement. The smartphone freed us from the constraints of the desktop computer only to ensure that the desktop's demands followed us into every waking moment. There is no automatic mechanism by which saved time converts into flourishing. That conversion requires intention, cultural infrastructure, and a shared understanding of what a good life looks like. These are precisely the things that a culture obsessed with technological capability tends to neglect.

The deeper challenge of AI is not economic but existential. What would it look like to take the relationship between technology and flourishing seriously? It would begin, I think, with the recognition that technological adoption is not inevitable in the way we often pretend it is. We make choices about which technologies to embrace, how deeply to integrate them, and what boundaries to maintain. # The Paradox of Capacity: Technology, Trade-offs, and What It Means to Flourish

There is a peculiar anxiety that accompanies abundance. A person standing before a wall of five hundred streaming options feels something quite different from a person settling into a theater seat in 1955, and it is not obviously better. This small, almost trivial observation points toward a much larger question that our civilization has been remarkably reluctant to examine with any rigor: Does the relentless expansion of technological capability actually make human lives go well?

The default assumption of modernity is that it does. We treat technological progress as roughly synonymous with human progress, and we have centuries of compelling evidence to support the conflation. Vaccines, sanitation, refrigeration, anesthesia—these are not trivial gains. They represent the elimination of suffering on a scale that would have seemed miraculous to our ancestors. Anyone tempted to romanticize pre-technological life should spend an afternoon reading accounts of pre-modern dentistry or childbirth. The case for technology as a force for human flourishing begins with the body, and at the level of the body, it is overwhelming.

But flourishing is not merely the absence of suffering, just as health is not merely the absence of disease. And it is precisely here—in the space between solving problems and living well—that the relationship between technology and human flourishing becomes genuinely complicated. While technology has proven indispensable in securing the material conditions for a good life, its unchecked expansion often undermines the psychological and existential conditions that flourishing equally requires. What follows is an argument not against technology, but for a more deliberate and philosophically serious relationship with our tools.

## The Instrumentalist Illusion

We tend to think of technologies as neutral instruments. A hammer can build a house or break a window; the moral weight belongs to the user, not the tool. This framework feels intuitive, and it is largely wrong. Technologies are not neutral. They carry within them assumptions about what matters, what deserves attention, and how time should be spent. They restructure incentives, reshape habits, and gradually remodel our cognitive and emotional patterns—conditioning us, for instance, to expect constant novelty, or to equate speed with value.

Consider the smartphone. Described instrumentally, it is a device that enables communication, provides access to information, and facilitates navigation. Described honestly, it is a technology that has fundamentally altered the texture of daily consciousness for billions of people. It has compressed the space between stimulus and response. It has made solitude functionally difficult. It has created an attentional environment of perpetual solicitation, interruption, and escape from whatever is immediately present.

None of this was the explicit intention of the smartphone's designers. It is simply what the technology does by virtue of what it is—a portal to an infinite feed of variable rewards, carried in the pocket, available at every moment. The philosopher of technology Langdon Winner argued decades ago that artifacts have politics. They also have psychologies. They shape the felt quality of experience whether we intend them to or not.

Some will object that the smartphone also deepens human connection—that it allows a grandmother to video-call her grandchildren across an ocean, or enables communities of shared interest to form across borders that would otherwise isolate. This is true, and it matters. But Sherry Turkle's research on digital communication suggests an important distinction between *connection* and *conversation*. The smartphone excels at the former: rapid, convenient, low-friction contact. It is considerably worse at fostering the latter: the slow, open-ended, sometimes uncomfortable exchange through which genuine intimacy and understanding develop. We have more connections than any generation in history, and an epidemic of loneliness. These two facts are not unrelated.

This does not mean the smartphone is a net negative. It means that adopting it involved a trade-off that most of us never consciously made. We gained extraordinary convenience and connectivity. We lost something harder to name—a certain quality of presence, an ease with stillness, a capacity for sustained attention that previous generations could take for granted. The trade-off may well be worth it. But it was a trade-off, and we should be honest about that.

## The Efficiency Trap

Modern technology is, above all, a project of optimization. It seeks to make processes faster, cheaper, more convenient, more frictionless. And optimization is genuinely valuable—right up to the point where it begins to erode the very things that make life meaningful.

This is because many of the experiences central to human flourishing are inherently inefficient. Learning a musical instrument is inefficient. Maintaining a deep friendship requires an extravagant expenditure of time that could be "better" spent. Raising children is, by any rational metric, a catastrophically poor allocation of resources. The things that constitute a rich human life—craft, relationship, contemplation, struggle, physical engagement with the material world—are almost universally slow, difficult, and resistant to optimization.

The philosopher Albert Borgmann captures this insight with his concept of "focal practices"—activities like cooking a meal over a fire, or walking to a destination, or playing music with others—that engage us fully, bodily and mentally, in a way that the technological alternatives specifically engineer away. Borgmann's point is not that we should reject devices, but that when devices replace focal practices entirely, something essential about human engagement with the world quietly disappears.

When technology optimizes away friction indiscriminately, it risks optimizing away meaning. The food delivery app that eliminates the need to cook also eliminates the sensory ritual of preparing a meal. The AI that generates a competent essay in seconds also removes the laborious process of thinking through a problem in prose—a process that, for the writer, is not merely a means to an end but a mode of understanding.

The food delivery app does not simply eliminate cooking; it eliminates the planning horizon, the intentionality, the small act of deciding what to nourish yourself with before the hunger arrives.

I am not making a Luddite argument. Difficulty is not inherently virtuous, and we should not preserve friction for its own sake—especially when that friction falls disproportionately on those with the fewest resources. I am suggesting that we need a more sophisticated framework for evaluating technological adoption than the simple question "Does this make things easier?" Sometimes the answer is yes, and the result is genuine human benefit. Sometimes the answer is yes, and the result is the quiet atrophying of a capacity we didn't realize we valued until it was gone.

## Flourishing in the Age of AI

These questions acquire new urgency with the emergence of artificial intelligence, and they acquire it because AI differs from previous technologies in kind rather than merely in degree. Earlier technologies substituted for human *labor*—the loom replaced the hand, the calculator replaced mental arithmetic. What was automated was the execution of tasks. But AI substitutes for something more fundamental: it substitutes for human *development*. The long, transformative process of becoming someone who can write clearly, compose music, diagnose a patient, or reason through a complex problem—this process of becoming is precisely what AI threatens to render optional.

This distinction matters enormously. When a machine digs a ditch, the human who would have dug it loses the exercise but not the capacity for growth. When a machine writes your arguments, analyzes your data, and solves your design problems, what atrophies is not just a skill but the developmental process by which you became a particular kind of thinker, a particular kind of person. Previous technologies substituted for outcomes. AI threatens to substitute for the transformative processes by which we become ourselves.

The optimistic vision is one of liberation. If AI can handle routine cognitive work, humans will be freed to pursue higher-order activities—creative expression, philosophical inquiry, deep relationship. This is essentially the same promise made about earlier labor-saving technologies, and it has occasionally been fulfilled. The washing machine genuinely did free up hours of domestic labor. Some of those hours were redirected toward education, civic engagement, and personal development.

But the historical record also shows that liberated time has a tendency to be captured—by new forms of work, by consumption, by entertainment designed to monetize attention. There is no automatic mechanism by which saved time converts into flourishing. That conversion requires intention, cultural infrastructure, and a shared understanding of what a good life looks like—precisely the things a culture obsessed with technological capability tends to neglect.

The deeper challenge is existential. If a machine can write a serviceable novel or compose a beautiful piece of music, what happens to the human motivation to attempt these things? Research in self-determination theory suggests that intrinsic motivation depends on feelings of competence, autonomy, and relatedness. But our sense of competence is not formed in isolation—it is constituted partly by difficulty and rarity. We value creative struggle in part because the struggle is genuinely hard and the achievement genuinely scarce. If AI makes creative production effortless and abundant, we cannot simply decide to value the process independently, because the valuation was partly constituted by the difficulty. This is not a problem that more technology solves. It is a problem that more technology deepens.

## Toward a More Deliberate Relationship

What would it look like to take the relationship between technology and flourishing seriously? It would begin with the recognition that technological adoption is not inevitable in the way we often pretend it is. We make choices about which technologies to embrace, how deeply to integrate them, and what boundaries to maintain. These choices are currently made almost entirely on the basis of convenience, cost, and competitive pressure. They could also be made on the basis of what kind of life, what kind of attention, what kind of community we want to cultivate.

This is not primarily a call for regulation, though regulation sometimes has a role. It is a call for a richer cultural conversation about ends rather than means. We are extraordinarily sophisticated in our thinking about what technology *can* do. We are remarkably impoverished in our thinking about what we *want*—not as consumers, but as human beings attempting to live lives of depth and purpose. That this question has become so difficult to answer is itself partly a technological effect: when the means of life are constantly revolutionized, the ends of life become harder to hold steady.

The *eudaimonia* the Greeks described was never about the accumulation of capability or the elimination of difficulty. It was about the development and exercise of distinctly human excellences: practical wisdom, courage, the capacity for deep friendship, the ability to perceive and create beauty. These excellences require certain conditions, including a degree of material security that technology can provide. But they also require struggle, limitation, embodied engagement, and the kind of sustained attention that our current technological environment actively undermines.

The path forward is a more deliberate, more philosophically informed relationship with technology. It means asking, before each adoption, not just "What does this enable?" but "What does this displace? What capacity does this allow to atrophy? What quality of experience does this foreclose?" It means treating convenience as one value among many, rather than as the supreme value before which all others must yield.

We have built a civilization of astonishing capability. We can edit genes, communicate instantaneously across the globe, and train machines to mimic the patterns of human thought. What we have not yet built is a wisdom adequate to these capabilities—a shared framework for deciding which powers to exercise, which to restrain, and how to preserve the conditions under which human beings can genuinely thrive. Whether we are still capable of building it—whether the sustained attention such work requires has not already atrophied beyond recovery—may be the question that determines what comes next.

# The Augmented Good Life: Technology, Trade-offs, and Human Flourishing

There is a particular kind of optimism that has dominated Western thought for at least two centuries—the conviction that technological progress and human progress are, if not identical, then at least reliably correlated. More capability means more freedom; more freedom means more flourishing. The logic feels almost gravitational. And yet, if you pause to examine your own lived experience in the most technologically saturated era in human history, the equation becomes far less obvious. We carry supercomputers in our pockets and report epidemic levels of loneliness. We have instant access to the sum of human knowledge and struggle to concentrate for more than a few minutes. We can speak to anyone on the planet and feel, somehow, less heard.

This is not an argument against technology. It is an argument for thinking more carefully about what we mean when we say a technology is *good*—and for whom, and under what conditions, and at what cost.

## The Capability Trap

The default assumption in most technology discourse is that increasing capability is inherently valuable. A faster processor, a more powerful model, a more efficient system—these are treated as self-evidently desirable. And in many cases, they are. Medical imaging that detects cancer earlier saves lives in ways that resist philosophical quibbling. Water purification technologies have done more to reduce human suffering than perhaps any moral philosophy ever written. The material gains of technological development are real, and any honest accounting of the relationship between technology and flourishing must begin by acknowledging them.

But capability is not the same as well-being. The distinction matters because it reveals a category error embedded in much techno-optimist thinking: the assumption that expanding what humans *can* do necessarily expands what humans *experience* as a good life. Aristotle's concept of eudaimonia—often translated as flourishing—was never primarily about capability. It was about the cultivation of virtues, the quality of relationships, the exercise of practical wisdom, and the integration of these into a coherent life. A life could be materially modest and still deeply flourishing. A life could be rich with tools and options and still spiritually impoverished.

This is not mere philosophical abstraction. Consider the research on the hedonic treadmill, which consistently demonstrates that increases in material comfort produce diminishing returns in subjective well-being beyond a certain threshold. Or consider the growing body of evidence linking heavy social media use to anxiety and depression, particularly among adolescents. The technology works exactly as designed—it connects, it informs, it entertains—and yet the human outcomes are, at best, ambiguous. The capability is extraordinary. The flourishing is uncertain.

## The Anatomy of Trade-offs

Every technology is a transaction. We gain something and we lose something, and the loss is often invisible at the moment of adoption because it operates on a different timescale or in a different register than the gain.

The automobile gave us unprecedented mobility and reshaped the physical and social geography of the modern world. It also gave us suburban isolation, sedentary lifestyles, catastrophic environmental damage, and the slow erosion of walkable communities where spontaneous human contact was the norm rather than the exception. These were not bugs in the system. They were structural consequences of a particular technological choice, consequences that took decades to become fully legible.

We are now in the early stages of a similar transaction with artificial intelligence and automation. The gains are already visible: AI systems that can diagnose diseases, optimize supply chains, generate creative work, and accelerate scientific research. These are genuine contributions to human capability, and in many domains they will reduce suffering and expand possibility. But the trade-offs deserve equally serious attention.

When AI systems begin to mediate more of our cognitive labor—writing, analysis, decision-making, even conversation—we risk atrophying the very capacities that make that labor meaningful. There is a difference between being relieved of drudgery and being relieved of effort altogether. The struggle to articulate a thought clearly, to reason through a complex problem, to craft language that captures something true about experience—these are not merely instrumental activities. They are constitutive of a certain kind of intellectual life. They are part of what it means to think, and thinking is not incidental to flourishing. It may be central to it.

This is not a Luddite argument. It is a recognition that human capacities are not fixed endowments but skills that develop through exercise and atrophy through neglect. The question is not whether AI can write a competent essay or solve a differential equation. Of course it can, and increasingly well. The question is what happens to the human being who never learns to do these things because the machine has made the effort unnecessary. What kind of mind develops in that environment? What kind of life does it support?

## The Meaning Problem

Perhaps the deepest challenge that advanced technology poses to human flourishing is not practical but existential. For most of human history, meaning was derived in large part from necessity—the need to grow food, build shelter, raise children, defend communities. Work was often brutal, but it was also legible. You could see the relationship between your effort and your survival, between your contribution and your community's well-being.

Automation has been steadily dissolving this relationship for over a century, and AI promises to accelerate the process dramatically. If machines can do most of what humans currently do for a living—and do it better, faster, and cheaper—then the question of what humans are *for* becomes not just philosophical but urgent. The optimistic answer is that we will be freed to pursue higher-order activities: art, philosophy, exploration, relationships. This is the Star Trek vision, and it is genuinely appealing.

But the historical evidence suggests that freedom from necessity does not automatically produce meaning. It can just as easily produce anomie, addiction, and despair. The opioid crisis in post-industrial American communities is not unrelated to the disappearance of meaningful work. The epidemic of what psychologist Martin Seligman calls "learned helplessness" is not unrelated to environments where individual agency feels irrelevant. Meaning, it turns out, is not what rushes in when obligation recedes. It must be actively constructed, and the construction requires skills, structures, and social conditions that technology alone cannot provide.

## Toward a More Honest Framework

None of this means we should resist technological development. That impulse, however understandable, is both impractical and intellectually dishonest—it ignores the genuine goods that technology delivers and romanticizes a past that was, for most people, defined by suffering that we are right to have escaped. The child who dies of a preventable disease does not benefit from our philosophical reservations about modernity.

What it means, instead, is that we need a more sophisticated framework for evaluating technology's relationship to flourishing—one that goes beyond the simple metric of capability and asks harder questions about the conditions under which human beings actually thrive.

Such a framework might begin with a few principles.

First, *technology should augment human agency rather than replace it*. The most beneficial technologies are those that expand what individuals can do while preserving their sense of authorship over their own lives. A tool that helps a doctor make better diagnoses is different in kind from a system that makes the doctor irrelevant. Both may produce good medical outcomes, but they have very different implications for the humans involved.

Second, *the social context of adoption matters as much as the technology itself*. The same technology can be liberating or oppressive depending on who controls it, who benefits from it, and what institutional structures govern its use. The internet is a different technology in a democracy with strong privacy protections than it is in an authoritarian surveillance state. AI is a different technology when it is deployed to augment workers than when it is deployed to eliminate them without any social safety net to absorb the shock.

Third, *we should be suspicious of technological solutions to problems that are fundamentally social or spiritual in nature*. Loneliness is not a connectivity problem. It is a problem of depth, vulnerability, and sustained attention—qualities that most communication technologies actively undermine. Depression is not an information problem. Meaning is not an optimization problem. When we treat these as engineering challenges, we misunderstand both the technology and the human condition.

Finally, *we should preserve spaces of deliberate inefficiency*. Not everything that can be optimized should be. The slow conversation, the handwritten letter, the walk without a podcast, the meal cooked without a recipe—these are not failures of productivity. They are practices that cultivate presence, patience, and a particular quality of attention that is essential to the good life. A world that optimizes all of these away in the name of efficiency will be a world that is very capable and very empty.

## Conclusion

The relationship between technology and human flourishing is not a simple function. It is not the case that more technology equals more flourishing, nor is it the case that technology is inherently alienating. The truth is more conditional and more interesting: technology contributes to flourishing when it is developed and deployed with a clear understanding of what flourishing actually requires—not just material comfort and expanded capability, but meaning, agency, deep relationships, and the ongoing exercise of distinctly human capacities.

We are entering an era of extraordinary technological power. The question that will define this era is not whether we *can* build increasingly capable systems. We obviously can. The question is whether we have the wisdom to build them in ways that serve not just our productivity or our convenience but our humanity. That is a question no algorithm can answer. It requires exactly the kind of slow, difficult, deeply human reflection that our fastest technologies are least equipped to provide—and that we, therefore, must be most deliberate about protecting.

The slow conversation, the handwritten letter, the walk without a podcast, the meal cooked without a recipe—these are not failures of productivity. They are practices that cultivate presence, patience, and a particular quality of attention that is essential to the good life. A world that optimizes all of these away in the name of efficiency will be a world that is very capable and very empty.

## Conclusion

The relationship between technology and human flourishing is not a simple function. More technology does not equal more flourishing, but neither is technology inherently alienating. The truth is more conditional and more interesting: technology contributes to flourishing when it is developed and deployed with a clear understanding of what flourishing actually requires—not just material comfort and expanded capability, but meaning, agency, deep relationships, and the ongoing exercise of distinctly human capacities.

We are entering an era of extraordinary technological power. The question that will define this era is not whether we *can* build increasingly capable systems. We obviously can. The question is whether we have the wisdom to build them in ways that serve not just our productivity or our convenience but our humanity.

And wisdom of that kind will not come from our fastest systems. It will come from the kind of thinking that looks, from the outside, like nothing at all: a person sitting in a chair, staring out a window, turning an unresolved question over in her mind without reaching for a device to answer it. # The Augmented Good Life: Technology, Trade-offs, and Human Flourishing

There is a particular kind of optimism that has dominated Western thought for at least two centuries—the conviction that technological progress and human progress are, if not identical, then at least reliably correlated. More capability means more freedom; more freedom means more flourishing. The logic feels almost gravitational. And yet, if you pause to examine your own lived experience in the most technologically saturated era in human history, the equation becomes far less obvious. We carry supercomputers in our pockets and report epidemic levels of loneliness. We have instant access to the sum of human knowledge and struggle to concentrate for more than a few minutes. We can speak to anyone on the planet and feel, somehow, less heard.

This is not an argument against technology. It is an argument that true human flourishing requires us to shift our technological calculus: capability must be subordinated to the cultivation of agency, meaning, and the deliberate exercise of human virtue. The question is not whether a technology is powerful, but whether it helps us become more fully ourselves.

## The Capability Trap

The default assumption in most technology discourse is that increasing capability is inherently valuable. A faster processor, a more powerful model, a more efficient system—these are treated as self-evidently desirable. And in many cases, they are. Medical imaging that detects cancer earlier saves lives in ways that resist philosophical quibbling. Water purification technologies have done more to reduce human suffering than perhaps any moral philosophy ever written. The material gains of technological development are real, and any honest accounting of the relationship between technology and flourishing must begin by acknowledging them.

But capability is not the same as flourishing. The distinction matters because it reveals a category error embedded in much techno-optimist thinking: the assumption that expanding what humans *can* do necessarily expands what humans *experience* as a good life. Aristotle's concept of *eudaimonia*—flourishing—was never primarily about capability. It was about the cultivation of virtues like courage and temperance, the exercise of practical wisdom in daily choices, and the integration of these into a coherent, purposeful life. A life could be materially modest and still deeply flourishing; a life rich with tools and options can still be spiritually impoverished.

This is not mere philosophical abstraction. Consider the research on the hedonic treadmill, which consistently demonstrates that increases in material comfort produce diminishing returns in subjective well-being beyond a certain threshold. Or consider the growing body of evidence linking heavy social media use to anxiety and depression, particularly among adolescents. The technology works exactly as designed—it connects, it informs, it entertains—and yet the human outcomes are, at best, ambiguous. The capability is extraordinary. The flourishing is uncertain.

I want to maintain this distinction throughout: when I say *flourishing*, I mean something richer and more demanding than subjective well-being or momentary satisfaction. I mean the Aristotelian sense—a life of purpose, depth, and active virtue. When I say *capability*, I mean the expansion of what is technically possible. These two things can move in concert, but they are not the same, and conflating them is the source of much confused thinking about technology.

## The Anatomy of Trade-offs

Every technology is a transaction. We gain something and we lose something, and the loss is often invisible at the moment of adoption because it operates on a different timescale or in a different register than the gain.

The automobile gave us unprecedented mobility and reshaped the physical and social geography of the modern world. It also gave us suburban isolation, sedentary lifestyles, catastrophic environmental damage, and the slow erosion of walkable communities where spontaneous human contact was the norm rather than the exception. These were not bugs in the system. They were structural consequences of a particular technological choice, consequences that took decades to become fully legible.

We are now in the early stages of a similar transaction with artificial intelligence and automation. The gains are already visible: AI systems that can diagnose diseases, optimize supply chains, generate creative work, and accelerate scientific research. These are genuine contributions to human capability, and in many domains they will reduce suffering and expand possibility. But the trade-offs deserve equally serious attention.

When AI systems begin to mediate more of our cognitive labor—writing, analysis, decision-making, even conversation—we risk atrophying the very capacities that make that labor meaningful. There is a difference between being relieved of drudgery and being relieved of effort altogether. The struggle to articulate a thought clearly, to reason through a complex problem, to craft language that captures something true about experience—these are not merely instrumental activities. They are constitutive of a certain kind of intellectual life. They are part of what it means to think, and thinking is not incidental to flourishing. It may be central to it.

This is not a Luddite argument. It is a recognition that human capacities are not fixed endowments but skills that develop through exercise and atrophy through neglect. The question is not whether AI can write a competent essay or solve a differential equation. Of course it can, and increasingly well. The question is what happens to the human being who never learns to do these things because the machine has made the effort unnecessary. What kind of mind develops in that environment? What kind of life does it support?

If the struggle required to master a skill is outsourced, we lose more than just efficiency; we lose the very structure through which purpose is often built. This leads us to the deepest challenge technology poses to human flourishing—not the practical question of what machines can do, but the existential question of what humans are for.

## The Meaning Problem

For most of human history, meaning was derived in large part from necessity—the need to grow food, build shelter, raise children, defend communities. Work was often brutal, but it was also legible. You could see the relationship between your effort and your survival, between your contribution and your community's well-being.

Automation has been steadily dissolving this relationship for over a century, and AI promises to accelerate the process dramatically. If machines can do most of what humans currently do for a living—and do it better, faster, and cheaper—then the question of what humans are *for* becomes not just philosophical but urgent. Optimists often counter the anxiety about displaced labor with structural solutions—universal basic income, shortened work weeks, expanded social safety nets—that would decouple survival from employment. Such economic scaffolding may well be necessary, and I do not dismiss it. But the historical evidence suggests that meaning is not merely a matter of material security; it is bound up with contribution, efficacy, and the felt sense that one's effort matters to someone. A guaranteed income addresses necessity, but it does not automatically solve the meaning problem that arises when one's effort feels irrelevant.

The opioid crisis in post-industrial American communities is not unrelated to the disappearance of meaningful work. The epidemic of what psychologist Martin Seligman calls "learned helplessness" is not unrelated to environments where individual agency feels beside the point. Meaning, it turns out, is not what rushes in when obligation recedes. It must be actively constructed, and the construction requires skills, structures, and social conditions that technology alone cannot provide.

None of this means we should resist technological development. That impulse, however understandable, is both impractical and intellectually dishonest—it ignores the genuine goods that technology delivers and romanticizes a past that was, for most people, defined by suffering that we are right to have escaped. The child who dies of a preventable disease does not benefit from our philosophical reservations about modernity.

Meaning is not an optimization problem. When we treat these as engineering challenges, we misunderstand both the technology and the human condition.

The slow conversation, the handwritten letter, the walk without a podcast, the meal cooked without a recipe—these are not failures of productivity. The relationship between technology and human flourishing is not a simple function. It is not the case that more technology equals more flourishing, nor is it the case that technology is inherently alienating. The truth is more conditional and more interesting: technology contributes to flourishing when it is developed and deployed with a clear understanding of what flourishing actually requires—not just material comfort and expanded capability, but meaning, agency, deep relationships, and the ongoing exercise of distinctly human capacities.
