Technology and human flourishing have always been entangled, but not in the simple way our slogans suggest. We are told—by marketing, by policy briefs, and sometimes by genuine optimism—that more capability means a better life: faster communication, cheaper goods, longer lifespans, richer entertainment, wider choice. These achievements are real, and in some cases morally decisive. It is difficult to romanticize a world without antibiotics, anesthesia, modern sanitation, or the agricultural and logistical systems that prevent mass famine.

Yet flourishing—what it means to live well—does not reduce to the quantity of options available or the speed with which we can satisfy preferences. It concerns the quality of our agency, the depth of our relationships, the meaningfulness of our contributions, the structure of our attention, and the moral texture of our communities. On these dimensions, technology is neither a straightforward ladder upward nor an unambiguous threat. It is an amplifier, a reorganizer, and sometimes a solvent.

A clear position follows from this: technological progress is best understood as an expansion of power, not an expansion of wisdom. Power can be used to build lives of greater freedom and dignity, or it can produce new forms of dependence and fragmentation. The decisive question is not whether technology advances—it will—but whether people and institutions cultivate the wisdom to steer new powers toward human ends rather than letting human ends be quietly rewritten around what our tools make easy.

## Capability is not the same as a better life

The strongest case for technological optimism begins with suffering. Over the last two centuries, technology has helped reduce infant mortality, shrink the burden of physical labor, expand access to education, and enable medicines that would have looked miraculous to earlier generations. It has made disasters more survivable and made information more available. A child living through a bacterial infection in 1880 and a child living through one today inhabit different moral universes, and technology is part of the difference.

But the leap from “technology can reduce suffering” to “more technological capability necessarily improves the human experience” does not hold. Flourishing is not simply living longer; it is having reason to want to. Nor is it merely having more choices; it is being able to choose well and to build a life one can endorse when the novelty wears off.

Even in wealthy societies saturated with technology, well-being does not climb in lockstep with capability. Many people report loneliness amid constant connectivity; anxiety amid unprecedented convenience; exhaustion in workplaces optimized for measurement; anger in public discourse engineered for engagement. These are not arguments for anti-technology nostalgia. They are reminders that lived experience is mediated: by culture, economics, design, and the incentives that decide what a tool is “for.”

A useful analogy is nutrition. Industrial food production increased calories and convenience, reducing famine in many places. But more calories did not automatically produce healthier bodies; in certain environments it produced obesity, diabetes, and disordered eating. The problem was not calories as such. It was a mismatch between a powerful new supply system and human biology, psychology, and regulation.

Technology can create the same mismatch. It often overfits to our short-term impulses—novelty, status, outrage, ease—while neglecting long-term goods that require patience, friction, and commitment. A world optimized to be frictionless can become a world where we lose beneficial frictions: the pauses that help us deliberate, the effort that builds competence, the inconveniences that make us rely on one another. Capability increases, but wisdom does not automatically rise with it.

## The trade-offs we make when we adopt new technologies

Every major technology is a bargain with consequences, and those consequences rarely remain confined to the domain the technology claims to improve. Adoption is not purely additive: it changes the ecology of everyday life—norms, incentives, skills, expectations. The benefits often arrive immediately and clearly; the costs creep in gradually, felt as mood, as family dynamics, as civic distrust. That temporal asymmetry biases societies toward adoption without reflection.

Three trade-offs are especially pervasive.

### Convenience can quietly erode agency

Many technologies promise to remove burdens. GPS removes the need to remember routes. Recommendation systems remove the need to search. Autocomplete removes the need to spell or even to finish a sentence. Increasingly, AI assistants remove the need to draft an email, outline an essay, or summarize a meeting.

Sometimes this is genuine liberation from drudgery. But it can also be a subtle form of outsourcing the self. Agency is not merely getting what we want; it is the capacity to form wants, revise them, and pursue them through effort that feels like one’s own. The more systems anticipate our choices, the more the “help” can become a narrowing of agency to mere selection among pre-chewed options.

A small, concrete image makes the point. Many email platforms now offer “smart replies”: three chirpy, ready-made sentences you can send with one tap—“Sounds great!” “Thanks for the update.” “Let’s do it.” They save time, and in certain contexts that is harmless. But they also change the texture of communication. If your gratitude and enthusiasm arrive as a default template, are you still speaking, or are you mostly choosing? Multiply that across days and relationships and you get something more than convenience: you get a new norm in which human expression becomes a set of menu options.

Friction is not always an enemy. The effort of planning, composing, and learning is part of how we develop competence and self-trust. There is a difference between being supported and being replaced—and the boundary matters for flourishing.

### Connectivity expands reach while thinning attention and intimacy

Communication technology collapses distance. That can deepen relationships, especially for people separated by geography, disability, or social constraints. It can also widen the circles within which we find peers, collaborators, or communities we would never meet locally.

But the same tools can erode intimacy through partial presence and perpetual interruption. Flourishing requires attention: sustained, selective, sometimes protected. Many digital platforms, however, monetize attention by fragmenting it—training users to check, skim, and react, and privileging emotionally arousing content because it keeps the feed moving.

The consequence is not merely “distraction,” as if attention were a private habit that some people lack. It is a change in the shape of experience. When a mind is trained to expect constant novelty, it becomes harder to do quiet, difficult things: reading deeply, listening without planning a response, enduring ambiguity, staying with another person’s pain when there is no quick fix. Relationships can become thinner or more performative, shaped by metrics of visibility rather than the slow accumulation of shared life.

Connectivity can be a bridge, but it can also become a solvent. The question is not whether we are connected, but whether our connection supports presence.

### Scale increases reach while diluting accountability

Technology allows actions to scale. One person can influence millions. A policy change can be implemented instantly across systems. An error can propagate everywhere, and so can a lie.

Scale brings obvious benefits: rapid dissemination of knowledge, efficient public services, global coordination in crises. But it also dilutes accountability. When harms occur, responsibility becomes hard to locate. Was it the engineer who built the model, the product manager who shipped it, the company that optimized engagement, the regulator who failed to act, the user who clicked “share”? Complexity and opacity can force people into dependence: they cannot contest decisions they cannot understand.

This matters because flourishing includes living under conditions one can question and influence. A technological environment that cannot be appealed to—where you are scored, sorted, throttled, or surveilled without meaningful recourse—is, in a political sense, infantilizing. It asks adults to accept decisions as weather.

## “But surely progress still trends toward flourishing?”

A serious defense of technological progress argues that capability does not guarantee flourishing but makes it more likely. Historically, many moral advances have been enabled by material and informational advances: literacy supports democratic participation; labor-saving devices free time; medical technology reduces the tyranny of disease; reproductive technology expands women’s autonomy. Moreover, some worries about technology recur with each generation—people feared the novel, the radio, the television—and yet societies adapt. In this view, the solution is not skepticism but inclusion: spread technology’s benefits more equitably so it becomes a platform for flourishing rather than a source of division.

This is a strong case, and any credible position must absorb it. The problem is not that technological optimism is foolish; it is that it underestimates how often the “learn to use it well” part fails by default. Adaptation is not automatic, and the interests shaping technological systems are not neutral. When business models reward addiction, surveillance, and polarization, the burden of adaptation falls on individuals—often the least resourced—who lack the time, information, or collective power to resist.

Telling people to “use it wisely” can be like telling them to “eat wisely” in a world engineered for cheap sugar and relentless marketing. It is not bad advice. It is simply not enough.

The deeper issue is that some technological changes do not merely add new options; they restructure the field of options. If public discourse is mediated by platforms that privilege engagement over truth, individuals cannot simply opt into a healthy epistemic environment. If hiring and lending are automated through opaque filters, a person cannot “choose” a world where decisions are legible. If work is automated in ways that hollow out stable livelihoods, it is cold comfort to say people have the “option” to retrain, especially when the training itself becomes another commodified treadmill.

Technological capability can be compatible with flourishing, but only when institutions align technology with human ends. Without that alignment, the ends themselves are quietly substituted: people come to want what is easy, to accept what is measured, and to call it progress.

## Flourishing in an age of AI and automation

AI and automation intensify these questions because they do not merely extend human muscles or memory. They increasingly compete with core human capacities: perception, language, prediction, and judgment. That makes it tempting to define flourishing as whatever machines cannot do—“authentic” human labor, “real” relationships, “unmediated” thought.

Purity, however, is not a workable standard. The printing press mediated thought; so did public schools; so does any language we inherit rather than invent. The more useful question is what human capacities deserve protection and cultivation, and what kinds of technological environments support them.

Four elements seem especially central.

### Meaningful agency: remaining authors of our lives

AI can enhance agency by reducing drudgery and widening access to expertise. A patient can understand medical terms; a student can get tutoring; a small business can draft contracts; a programmer can offload boilerplate. These are genuine expansions of power at the individual level.

But AI can also diminish agency by turning life into an endless stream of suggestions. If your calendar auto-prioritizes tasks, your news feed anticipates your politics, your entertainment queue predicts your moods, and your writing assistant smooths your voice into a generic competence, you may remain “productive” while becoming less self-directed. A life of constant optimization can become a life where ends are silently chosen for you.

Flourishing requires the ability to set ends, not merely receive recommendations for efficient means. That implies design norms that preserve legibility and contestability: people should know when an AI is nudging them, what it is optimizing for, and how to override it. It also implies education that treats AI not as an oracle but as a tool—powerful, fallible, and shaped by incentives.

### Dignified contribution: being useful to one another, not just employed

Automation will likely increase productivity. But productivity gains do not automatically translate into dignified lives. Work, in the broad sense, is not only a way to earn; it is a source of structure, mastery, recognition, and contribution. Many people flourish not because their jobs are glamorous, but because someone relies on them—and they can see the dependence.

The “post-work” counterargument deserves more respect than it often gets. For many, “dignified work” has historically been drudgery: dangerous factories, humiliating service roles, pointless bureaucratic churn. A world with less compulsory labor could be a moral improvement, especially if it frees people for caregiving, learning, art, and community.

The catch is that our current economic model recognizes usefulness mainly through paid jobs, and our status systems often follow the same logic. If automation removes jobs without replacing the social pathways through which people feel needed, we risk producing not leisure but listlessness—income without belonging, time without purpose, freedom without a role in anyone else’s life.

So the target should not be “employment at all costs.” It should be dignified contribution: a society where people can develop competence and be useful to one another in ways that are socially recognized and materially supported. That may require new institutions—stronger public options for care work, civic projects, apprenticeships, artistic patronage, or forms of social insurance that do not treat non-market contribution as failure. The problem AI poses is not merely economic displacement. It is a crisis of social meaning if we let “job” remain the only recognized proof of value.

### Epistemic integrity: living in a world we can know together

AI-generated content, deepfakes, and personalized persuasion threaten the conditions under which people share reality. Flourishing depends on trust: in institutions, in one another, and in the basic reliability of what we see and hear. If the informational environment becomes so polluted that ordinary citizens cannot distinguish genuine testimony from synthetic manipulation, civic life deteriorates.

The result is not merely misinformation; it is cynicism. People stop arguing about what is true and start assuming everything is propaganda. They withdraw, or they cling to tribal narratives because shared reality feels unavailable.

Protecting epistemic integrity will require technical measures—provenance standards, authentication, watermarking, and auditability—but it will also require institutional and cultural reforms. Newsrooms, schools, courts, scientific bodies, and platforms all become more important, not less, in an era when “seeing is believing” no longer holds. A flourishing society is one where truth can still be a public good, not merely a private preference.

### Moral and civic responsibility: systems we can answer for

AI systems increasingly make or shape decisions with moral weight: who gets hired, who receives loans, who is flagged for surveillance, who receives medical attention first, whose speech is amplified or suppressed. Flourishing in such a world requires that the systems be governable.

That means transparency where possible, accountability mechanisms where not, and democratic oversight over high-stakes deployments. It also means resisting a common abdication: “the algorithm decided.” Humans decide to deploy the algorithm; humans choose its objectives; humans tolerate its errors because they find the trade-off convenient or profitable. A society that flourishes is one in which people remain responsible for the norms encoded in their tools.

## What should we do with this power?

Diagnosing the mismatch is easier than fixing it. It is simpler to notice that attention is fragmented than to build an economy that does not profit from fragmentation. It is easier to warn about automation than to redesign institutions of work and recognition. Still, a path forward exists if we adopt a more demanding standard for technological adoption: judge technologies not only by efficiency and novelty, but by the kinds of people and societies they tend to produce.

Three shifts would help.

First, societies should treat attention, privacy, and autonomy as public goods, not merely individual preferences. When an economy profits from surveillance and compulsion, it is rational for companies to erode these goods even if individuals “consent.” Regulation can be freedom-preserving when it prevents exploitative designs that convert human vulnerability into revenue—much as food regulation aims to make “eat wisely” feasible rather than heroic.

Second, we should build “human infrastructure” alongside technical infrastructure—and name what it is for: the cultivation of wisdom. If technology expands power, wisdom is the capacity to use power well: to choose ends worth pursuing, to see long-term consequences, to resist manipulation, to deliberate together, and to remain responsible for what we build. Education that teaches critical thinking and emotional resilience is not a luxury. Public spaces that support community are not nostalgia. Labor policies that smooth transitions are not mere economics. These are the cultural and institutional forms by which societies convert capability into flourishing rather than into drift.

AI literacy, in particular, should include not only how to prompt a model, but how to question it: What is this system optimized for? What data shaped it? Where does it fail? Who benefits when I rely on it?

Third, we should place decisions as close as feasible to the people affected—a principle of subsidiarity for technology. Not every system can be decentralized, but governance can be participatory. Local communities, professional associations, and worker councils can have meaningful roles in how automation is deployed in schools, hospitals, and workplaces. The goal is not to freeze progress. It is to ensure that progress remains answerable.

Underlying these practical steps is a deeper cultural choice: recover a richer vocabulary of flourishing. If the good life is defined as maximal convenience and minimal discomfort, technology will naturally become an engine for narcotizing ease. But if flourishing includes virtues—patience, courage, honesty, generosity—then we can ask better questions about design and adoption. GPS is not bad; a life that forgets the joy of orientation might be. Smart Reply is not evil; a culture that cannot speak without templates might be. AI assistance is not a betrayal; a professional world that devalues human judgment and treats people as mere operators might be.

## Conclusion

Increasing technological capability expands what human beings can do, but it does not tell us what we should do, what we should value, or what kind of lives are worth building. The modern temptation is to treat capability as destiny: if a thing can be built, it will be; if it improves metrics, it must be progress. But flourishing is not a metric to be optimized by remote systems. It is a lived achievement, dependent on agency, community, meaning, and responsibility.

Technology expands power. The open question—political, cultural, moral—is whether we will expand wisdom to match it. In an age of AI and automation, the central task is to insist that technology remain a means rather than becoming an environment that silently redefines our ends. That will require more than personal discipline. It will require institutions that align incentives with human goods, designs that respect autonomy, and a politics willing to distribute benefits and govern harms.

The future can be one in which technology helps people flourish. But it will not happen by default, and it will not happen simply because we can build more. It will happen only if flourishing—guided by wisdom—becomes the standard by which we decide what we build, what we deploy, and what we refuse.

Many technologies promise to remove burdens: navigation removes the need to remember routes, recommendation systems remove the need to search, automation removes the need to perform repetitive tasks. Often this is a gift. But it can also erode skills and narrow agency.

Agency is not merely getting what one wants. It is the capacity to form wants, to revise them, and to pursue them through effort that feels like one’s own. When systems anticipate our choices, “help” can become a subtle form of outsourcing the self. That sentence may sound dramatic, but the phenomenon is mundane: if every uncertainty is met with a suggestion, the muscle of choosing weakens; if every boredom is met with stimulation, the capacity to endure quiet diminishes; if every problem is met with a tool that makes the hard part vanish, competence becomes less a lived achievement than a subscription.

Friction is not always the enemy. The effort of planning a route, choosing a book without an algorithmic nudge, learning a skill rather than relying on a shortcut—these are not merely inefficient detours. They are part of how we develop mastery and self-trust. There is a difference between being supported and being replaced.

### 2) Connectivity vs. attention and intimacy

Communication technology collapses distance. That can deepen relationships, especially for those separated by geography, disability, migration, or social constraint. It can create communities where none were possible before. Yet the same tools can erode intimacy through partial presence and perpetual interruption.

Flourishing requires attention: sustained, selective, sometimes protected. Many digital platforms, however, monetize attention by fragmenting it—rewarding compulsive checking, privileging emotionally arousing content, and turning social life into a feed. The consequence is not merely distraction; it is a shift in the shape of experience. When the mind is trained to skim and react, the ability to do difficult, quiet things—reading deeply, listening carefully, enduring ambiguity—atrophies.

Relationships, too, can become thinner or more anxious, shaped by metrics of visibility rather than the slow accumulation of shared life. A life can be “connected” and still feel lonely. That is not a paradox; it is the predictable result of confusing contact with communion.

### 3) Scale vs. accountability

Technology allows actions to scale: one person can influence millions; decisions can be implemented instantly across systems; errors can propagate widely. Scale brings benefits—rapid dissemination of knowledge, efficient services—but it dilutes accountability.

When harms occur, responsibility becomes hard to locate: was it the designer, the company, the user, the regulator, the model? And when systems become complex and opaque, people are pushed into dependence. They cannot contest decisions they cannot understand—whether those decisions concern credit, hiring, insurance, parole, medical triage, or what information is placed before their eyes. Flourishing includes living under conditions one can contest and influence. An unaccountable technological environment is, in a political sense, infantilizing.

None of this implies that adoption is irrational or that we should retreat into nostalgia. It means adoption is never purely additive. The new tool changes the ecology of life: norms, incentives, skills, expectations. And the costs often appear gradually—felt as mood, as family dynamics, as civic distrust—while the benefits arrive immediately. That temporal asymmetry biases societies toward adoption without reflection.

## Why capability might still trend toward flourishing

A serious defense of technological progress argues that capability does not guarantee flourishing but makes it more likely by reducing suffering and expanding options. Historically, many moral and political advances have been enabled by material and informational advances: literacy supports democratic participation; labor-saving devices free time for education and civic life; medical technology reduces the tyranny of disease; reproductive technology expands women’s autonomy. Moreover, some fears repeat with each generation—people worried that novels would corrupt the mind, that radio would make conversation disappear, that television would rot attention—and societies often do adapt. Better to have powerful tools and learn to use them well, this view suggests, than to restrain progress and accept preventable suffering. When technology harms, the remedy is not skepticism but inclusion: spread the benefits equitably so technology becomes a platform for flourishing rather than a source of division.

This is a strong argument, and any credible position must absorb it. The problem is not that technological optimism is naïve; it is that it treats “we will learn to use it well” as the default outcome. Adaptation is not automatic, and the interests shaping technological systems are not neutral. When business models reward addiction, surveillance, and polarization, the burden of adaptation falls on individuals who lack the time, information, and collective power to resist. Telling people to “use it wisely” is like telling them to “eat wisely” in a world engineered for cheap sugar and constant marketing—sound advice, inadequate governance.

More deeply, some technological changes do not simply add options; they restructure the field of options. If work is automated in ways that hollow out livelihoods and local economies, it is cold comfort to say people have the “option” to retrain. If public discourse is mediated by platforms that privilege engagement over truth, individuals cannot simply opt into a healthier epistemic environment. The optimistic argument succeeds where institutions align technology with human ends. It fails where the ends are quietly substituted.

## Flourishing in an age of AI and automation

AI intensifies every trade-off above because it scales not only force and speed but interpretation. It is increasingly woven into how we communicate, how we learn, how we are evaluated, and how decisions are made about us. It is tempting, therefore, to define flourishing against AI: to insist that what matters is “authentic” human labor, “real” relationships, “unmediated” thought. But purity is not a workable standard. The printing press mediated thought; so did public schools; so does any language we inherit rather than invent. The more useful question is: what capacities deserve protection and cultivation, and what kinds of technological environments support them?

A plausible account of flourishing in the age of AI includes at least four elements.

### 1) Meaningful agency: being an author of one’s life

AI can enhance agency by reducing drudgery and widening access to expertise: drafting assistance, translation, tutoring, medical pattern recognition, adaptive tools for disability. Used well, it can expand what ordinary people can attempt.

But it can also diminish agency by nudging, predicting, and optimizing us into passivity. If your world is curated so thoroughly that you rarely confront the need to choose—what to read, whom to trust, what to attempt, how to interpret your own feelings—your life may become easier while becoming less yours. This is not dystopian science fiction. It is the quiet path of least resistance.

Flourishing requires that people retain the ability to set ends, not merely receive recommendations for efficient means. That implies design norms that keep choice architectures legible and contestable, and social norms that value deliberation over frictionless consumption. It also implies education that treats AI not as an oracle but as a tool—powerful, fallible, shaped by incentives.

### 2) Dignified work: contribution, not just income

Automation will likely increase productivity. Productivity gains, however, do not automatically translate into dignified lives. Work is not only a way to earn; it is a source of social recognition, structure, mastery, and contribution. Many jobs are degrading or pointless, and it would be a moral victory to eliminate drudgery. But a society that replaces human roles without providing alternative pathways to contribution risks producing not leisure, but despair.

The familiar counterargument says “work is overrated.” The stronger version—especially in AI discourse—is utopian: AI could solve scarcity itself, creating a post-scarcity world in which basic flourishing is guaranteed and contribution becomes purely voluntary self-expression. There is something noble in this vision. It refuses the old moralism that equates worth with wage labor.

Yet it often overlooks two stubborn realities. First, structured effort is a psychological need for many people: not constant toil, but a discipline that anchors the day and offers measurable growth. Leisure without community, without purpose, without recognition can become isolation. Second, even if abundance is technically possible, distributing it is politically difficult. A post-scarcity economy can still produce hierarchies—of control over systems, of status, of access to meaning-making institutions—creating new dependencies even as material poverty declines.

So the challenge is not merely technical. It is political and cultural: how to distribute gains, how to redesign labor markets, how to honor caregiving and civic work, and how to create institutions where people can develop competence and be needed.

### 3) Epistemic integrity: living in a world that can be known

AI-generated text, deepfakes, and personalized persuasion threaten the conditions under which people can share reality. Flourishing depends on trust: in institutions, in one another, and in the basic reliability of what we see and hear. If the informational environment becomes so polluted that ordinary citizens cannot distinguish genuine testimony from synthetic manipulation, civic life deteriorates. The result is not just being misinformed; it is becoming cynical. Cynicism is a kind of civic depression: the conviction that truth is inaccessible, so withdrawal is rational.

Protecting epistemic integrity will require technical measures (provenance standards, watermarking, authentication) and institutional reforms (platform accountability, campaign rules, journalism support). It will also require cultural habits that reward truth over virality—habits that technology can either undermine or reinforce.

### 4) Moral and civic responsibility: systems we can answer for

AI systems increasingly make or shape decisions with moral weight: who gets hired, who receives loans, who is flagged for investigation, who is shown what news, who is denied an appeal. Flourishing in such a world requires that systems be governable. That means transparency where possible, accountability mechanisms where not, and democratic oversight over high-stakes deployments.

It also means resisting a common abdication: “the algorithm decided.” Algorithms do not absolve us; they concentrate our values—often without our noticing—into repeatable form. A flourishing society is one in which humans remain responsible for the norms encoded in their tools.

These four elements—agency, contribution, integrity, and responsibility—are precisely what the earlier trade-offs threaten to erode. Convenience can diminish agency. Connectivity can fracture attention and intimacy. Scale can dissolve accountability. AI magnifies all three dynamics, which is why the stakes feel newly urgent.

## What should we do with this?

If flourishing is a cultivated achievement rather than an optimized outcome, then our response must shift from passive acceptance of technological momentum to active, normative stewardship. The point is not to halt innovation. It is to raise the standard by which we judge it: not only by efficiency or novelty, but by the kinds of lives and societies it tends to produce.

Three practical commitments follow.

First, we should treat attention, privacy, and autonomy as public goods, not merely individual preferences. When an economy profits from surveillance and compulsion, it is rational for firms to erode these goods even if individuals “consent.” Regulation can be freedom-preserving when it prevents exploitative designs that convert human vulnerability into revenue—dark patterns, addictive mechanics, opaque profiling, and markets in intimate data.

Second, we should build “human infrastructure” alongside technical infrastructure: education that teaches critical thinking and emotional resilience; public spaces that support community; labor policies that smooth transitions; cultural institutions that offer meaning beyond consumption. AI literacy should include not only how to use tools, but how to question them: What is this system optimized for? What data trained it? What is it blind to? Who benefits from my reliance on it?

Third, we should adopt a principle of subsidiarity for technology: place decisions and control as close as feasible to the people affected. Not every system can be fully decentralized, but governance can still be participatory. Professional associations, worker councils, and local communities can have a voice in how automation is deployed—especially in high-stakes settings like education, medicine, hiring, and policing. The goal is not to freeze progress. It is to keep progress answerable.

Underlying all three commitments is a cultural task: recovering a richer vocabulary of flourishing. If the good life is defined as maximal convenience and minimal discomfort, then technology will naturally become an engine for narcotizing ease. But if flourishing includes virtues—patience, courage, honesty, generosity—then we can ask how tools support or undermine those virtues. A navigation app is not bad; a life so dependent on it that we lose the pleasure of orientation might be. A recommendation system is not bad; a culture that cannot choose without being nudged is. AI assistance is not bad; a professional world that treats humans as mere operators of opaque systems is.

## Conclusion

Increasing technological capability expands what human beings can do. It does not, by itself, tell us what we should do, what we should value, or what kind of lives are worth building. The modern temptation is to treat capability as destiny: if a thing can be built, it will be; if it improves metrics, it must be progress. But human flourishing is not a metric to be optimized by remote systems. It is a lived achievement—dependent on agency, community, meaning, and responsibility.

In an age of AI and automation, the central task is to insist that technology remain a means rather than becoming an environment that silently redefines our ends. That insistence cannot rest on personal discipline alone, because the pressures are structural and the incentives are designed. It will require institutions that align technological power with human goods, designs that respect autonomy, and a politics willing to distribute benefits and govern harms.

The future can be one in which technology helps people flourish. But it will not happen automatically. Power expands on its own. Wisdom must be built.

A new app delivers convenience on day one; the downstream reshaping of attention, norms, and institutions emerges slowly enough to feel like personal failure rather than systemic design.

## The strongest case for optimism—and what it misses

A serious defense of technological progress does not claim that capability guarantees flourishing. It claims something subtler: that capability makes flourishing more likely by reducing suffering and expanding feasible life paths. Historically, many moral and political advances have been enabled by material and informational advances. Literacy supports democratic participation. Electricity and appliances reduce backbreaking domestic labor. Medical technology loosens the grip of disease. Reproductive technology expands women’s autonomy. In the long run, productivity gains have often raised living standards across much of the distribution, even if the gains arrive unevenly and after painful transitions.

There is also an argument from historical adaptation. Societies have repeatedly absorbed disruptive technologies—printing, industrial machinery, electricity, radio, television, the internet—and eventually developed norms, regulations, and cultural practices that captured many benefits while mitigating the worst harms. Child labor was not abolished by rejecting industrialization but by governing it. Food became safer not by abandoning mass production but by building inspection regimes, standards, and accountability. On this view, it is better to have powerful tools and learn to use them well than to restrain progress and accept preventable suffering.

This is not a straw man; it is a strong empirical and moral case. The problem is not that adaptation never happens. The problem is that adaptation is not guaranteed, and the conditions that make it likely—time, institutional capacity, and aligned incentives—are increasingly strained. “Use it wisely” is good advice, but it is inadequate as policy in environments engineered to exploit human vulnerabilities. Telling individuals to manage their attention in an economy that sells attention is like telling consumers to “eat wisely” in a world designed around cheap sugar and omnipresent marketing: possible for some, punishing for many, and structurally mismatched.

The deeper question is whether AI represents a disruption that breaks the historical pattern, or at least stresses it in a new way. There are reasons to think it might.

First, AI targets cognitive labor, not only physical labor. Previous waves of automation substituted for muscle and routine procedure; they also created large new categories of middle-skill work in administration, services, and knowledge management. AI reaches into the very domains that became the refuge and engine of the modern middle class: writing, design, analysis, tutoring, coding, basic legal work, triage, and planning. When the contested terrain is “thinking work” itself, the transition may not simply shift workers from one set of tasks to another; it may compress entire ladders of apprenticeship and professional identity.

Second, AI changes faster than many institutions can respond. Electricity and industrial machinery diffused over decades; major regulatory and cultural adaptations could lag without being instantly fatal. AI systems update weekly, deploy globally, and can be integrated into products with near-zero marginal cost. That speed matters. The slower the institutional response relative to the technology’s diffusion, the more the default business model becomes the de facto constitution.

Third, AI systems are unusually good at persuasion and personalization. The risk is not only job displacement or isolated bias; it is a continuous, scalable capacity to shape beliefs and behavior—advertising and propaganda with feedback loops, optimized in real time. Earlier media certainly influenced societies, but AI can individualize influence at scale.

None of this proves that AI will reduce flourishing. It does suggest that relying on “we’ll adapt like we always do” is not a plan; it is a hope. The question becomes: what would it mean to steer this power toward human ends?

## What flourishing should mean in the age of AI

If progress is power without wisdom, then wisdom is the missing ingredient—and we should be clear about what it is. Wisdom is not a vibe or a moral slogan; it is embodied in practices and institutions that help people choose well together: education that builds judgment, labor markets that dignify contribution, media environments that reward truth, and governance that makes power answerable.

In the age of AI and automation, flourishing requires at least four things.

### 1) Meaningful agency: remaining the author, not the optimized object

AI can enhance agency by reducing drudgery and widening access to expertise. A good tool can help a non-native speaker write clearly, a patient understand a diagnosis, a small business draft contracts, a student test ideas. Used well, AI can widen the circle of competence.

But AI also tends to reduce agency when it becomes the default intermediary between person and world—when it predicts, nudges, and optimizes us into passivity. The danger is not that a model answers questions; it is that the human stops asking their own. Flourishing requires that people retain the ability to set ends, not merely receive recommendations for efficient means.

That implies design and policy norms that protect legibility and choice. If an AI system recommends what you read, watch, buy, or believe, the criteria should be contestable—not a proprietary fog. It also implies education that treats AI not as an oracle but as a tool: powerful, fallible, and shaped by incentives. “AI literacy” should include basic technical understanding, yes, but also civic understanding: What is this system optimized for? Who pays? What data trained it? What does it systematically miss?

### 2) Dignified contribution: more than income, less than nostalgia

Automation will likely increase productivity. The optimistic story says this is how societies get richer and freer: fewer hours of necessary labor, more time for family, art, and learning. That possibility is real, and it is under-discussed in a culture that treats work as the only legitimate source of meaning. If AI takes over certain forms of cognitive drudgery—scheduling, summarizing, drafting, routine documentation—human attention could be freed for precisely the things that constitute flourishing: patient listening, careful mentoring, creative risk, community building, moral deliberation. The optimistic scenario is not that humans do nothing; it is that humans do more of what only humans are good for, or what humans uniquely value.

But that scenario is not self-executing. Work is not only a way to earn; it is also a source of structure, mastery, social recognition, and contribution. A society that replaces roles faster than it builds new pathways to contribution risks producing not leisure but despair. The transition costs—dislocation, status loss, community erosion—are not incidental; they are moral harms that can last a generation.

Flourishing, then, requires institutions that distribute the gains and preserve the dignity of being needed. That may mean wage insurance, stronger bargaining power, portable benefits, and serious public investment in training that is connected to real demand. It may also mean expanding what counts as valued contribution: caregiving, civic work, and community building are productive in the deepest sense, even when markets underpay them. If AI increases social wealth, a flourishing society uses that wealth to make contribution broadly available—not only to owners of capital and a thin layer of elite professionals.

### 3) Epistemic integrity: a world that can be jointly known

Flourishing is impossible in a hall of mirrors. If people cannot distinguish genuine testimony from synthetic manipulation, they lose not only information but trust—the quiet background confidence that makes cooperation possible. AI-generated content, deepfakes, automated comment farms, and personalized persuasion threaten the conditions under which citizens can share reality.

The response cannot be a single technical fix, but technical measures matter. Provenance standards—ways to authenticate where an image or video came from—should become normal for high-stakes contexts (elections, courts, major news). Watermarking and cryptographic signing will not eliminate deception, but they can raise the cost of mass manipulation and give institutions a basis for verification. Platforms should be pressured—by regulation and by public demand—to label synthetic media, reduce algorithmic amplification of unverified viral content, and allow meaningful independent auditing.

Yet epistemic integrity is also cultural. A flourishing society cultivates norms that reward correction over dunking, and institutions that earn trust through transparency and competence. In a polluted information environment, cynicism feels sophisticated; it is actually a form of surrender. Protecting a knowable world is part of protecting the possibility of shared self-government.

### 4) Accountable governance: systems we can answer for

AI systems increasingly make or shape decisions with moral weight: who gets hired, who receives loans, who is surveilled, who is denied insurance, who is flagged as suspicious. In such a world, “the algorithm decided” becomes a tempting abdication. Flourishing requires the opposite posture: systems must remain answerable to the people who live under them.

That means enforceable accountability in high-stakes domains: documentation requirements, bias and safety testing, avenues for appeal, and human responsibility that is not ceremonial. It also means a principle of subsidiarity: decisions and control should sit as close as feasible to the people affected. Not every system can be fully decentralized, but governance can be participatory—through worker councils shaping workplace automation, professional associations setting standards for AI in medicine or law, and local communities having a say in surveillance deployments.

Power without wisdom becomes power without responsibility. The only durable alternative is governance that makes power contestable.

## A more demanding standard for “progress”

If technological capability does not guarantee flourishing, the response is not Luddite rejection. It is a more demanding standard for adoption: technologies should be judged not only by efficiency and novelty, but by the kinds of lives and societies they tend to produce.

That standard shifts what we treat as negotiable. Attention, privacy, and autonomy are not merely individual preferences; they are public goods. When an economy profits from surveillance and compulsion, it is rational for companies to erode these goods even when users “consent,” because consent is manufactured through design and necessity. Regulation can preserve freedom when it prevents exploitative architectures that turn human vulnerability into revenue.

It also shifts what we build alongside technology. Roads and servers are not enough. Societies need “human infrastructure”: education that builds judgment and resilience; public spaces that support community rather than consumption; labor policies that smooth transitions and preserve dignity; cultural institutions that offer meaning outside the marketplace. Without this scaffolding, the power we gain becomes a force that scatters rather than supports us.

Finally, it requires a richer vocabulary of flourishing. If the good life is defined as maximal convenience and minimal discomfort, technology will naturally become an engine for narcotizing ease. But if flourishing includes virtues—patience, courage, honesty, generosity—then we can ask better questions of our tools. A navigation app is not a moral failure; a life in which we lose the pleasure of orientation might be. A recommendation system is not inherently corrosive; a culture that cannot choose without being nudged is. AI assistance is not dehumanizing by definition; a professional world that devalues human judgment and treats people as mere operators is.

## Conclusion

Increasing technological capability expands what human beings can do, but it does not tell us what we should do, what we should value, or what kind of lives are worth building. The modern temptation is to treat capability as destiny: if a thing can be built, it will be; if it improves metrics, it must be progress. But flourishing is not a metric to be optimized by remote systems. It is a lived achievement, dependent on agency, community, meaning, and responsibility.

Technology will continue to amplify human power. The question is whether we will build the wisdom—through norms, institutions, and governance—to keep that power in service of human ends. The future can be one in which technology helps people flourish—but only if flourishing, rather than capability alone, becomes the standard by which we judge what we build.

Technology and human flourishing have always been entangled, but not in the simple way our slogans suggest. We are told—sometimes by marketing, sometimes by sincere optimism—that more capability means a better life: faster communication, cheaper goods, longer lifespans, richer entertainment, wider choice. Many of these are genuine achievements. It is hard to look at antibiotics, modern sanitation, disaster forecasting, or accessible education and argue that human beings were, in general, better positioned to live well without them.

But flourishing is not the same thing as capability. Flourishing names a thicker accomplishment: the ability to author a life one can endorse; to sustain relationships that are not merely frequent but deep; to do work that grants recognition and meaning; to inhabit an informational world that can be trusted; to have attention that is not constantly seized from the outside. Technology can support these conditions. It can also dissolve them.

My central claim is that technological progress is best understood as an expansion of power, not an expansion of wisdom. Power is morally indeterminate: it can relieve suffering and widen freedom, or it can produce new dependencies and new forms of fragmentation. And because power now arrives packaged in institutions—platforms, labor markets, surveillance infrastructures, automated bureaucracies—whether technology serves flourishing is not a matter of personal virtue alone. It is a matter of design, incentives, and governance. If capability does not automatically produce flourishing, then steering capability toward human ends is not optional. It is constitutive of progress itself.

To make that less panoramic and more consequential, consider a single, increasingly ordinary scenario.

### A case: the automated gatekeeper

A large hospital system adopts an AI triage and scheduling tool. On paper, its purpose is unambiguously humane: reduce wait times, allocate scarce clinician hours, identify high-risk patients earlier, and save money that can be redirected to care. The model is trained on years of historical data—appointments kept and missed, diagnoses given, medications filled, outcomes recorded. It performs impressively in pilot studies. Administrators see graphs and forecasts. The tool is deployed.

Soon, a pattern emerges. Some patients—especially those with unstable housing, limited transportation, inconsistent phone access, or jobs with unpredictable hours—are flagged as “high no-show risk.” The system begins to schedule them less often, or it assigns them to lower-priority slots, or it requires additional confirmations. Another group—patients with complicated chronic conditions whose records are messy—gets routed into longer queues because the model “learns” that their appointments are likely to run over time.

No one in the chain feels malicious. The scheduler blames the system: it is “optimizing.” The hospital points to efficiency metrics: overall wait times are down. Clinicians are relieved that their days are less chaotic. From the standpoint of capability, this looks like progress: a complex operation is running more smoothly.

From the standpoint of flourishing, something more ambiguous has happened. A tool introduced to increase access may be quietly rationing care according to predictability, not need; according to legibility to the system, not dignity as a person. The patients most likely to be excluded are those whose lives already carry the heaviest burdens—precisely those for whom healthcare could most improve the conditions of living well.

This is the power-without-wisdom problem in miniature. The system has learned patterns, but it has not learned justice. It scales decisions, but it blurs accountability. It makes life easier for the institution, but it may make life less governable for the people most affected by it.

And crucially: once such a system is integrated, it stops being a tool you can simply decline. It becomes the environment. You can no longer opt out of the logic that sorts you.

That is what is at stake when we ask whether increasing technological capability necessarily improves the human experience. It often improves *some* experiences. It often improves *average* metrics. But it can simultaneously degrade the conditions that make a society worth living in—especially for those with the least power to contest how the tool works.

### Capability is not the same as a better life

The optimistic story about technology is not wrong. It is incomplete. It says: with more capability, we can reduce suffering and expand options; therefore, experience tends to improve. But flourishing is not merely living longer; it is having reason to want to. Nor is it merely having more options; it is having the ability to choose well and to commit to choices without being continuously manipulated or undermined.

We already know this from domains less politically charged than AI. The industrialization of food production increased calories and convenience, reducing famine in many places. But more calories did not automatically produce healthier bodies. In some environments, it produced diabetes, obesity, and a daily low-grade struggle against engineered appetites. The mismatch was not between “food” and “health” in the abstract, but between a powerful supply system and human biology, psychology, and regulation. We learned—slowly, unevenly—that “personal responsibility” is not a sufficient public-health strategy in a world designed for cheap sugar and constant marketing.

Digital technology generalizes this mismatch. Many systems are optimized for short-term impulses—novelty, outrage, status, ease—because those are profitable signals. In that setting, individual self-control is real but overmatched. The question is not whether technology is “good” or “bad,” but whether the surrounding institutions align technological incentives with long-term human goods.

This is why capability and flourishing can diverge so sharply in wealthy, technologically saturated societies. We can be surrounded by conveniences and still suffer from loneliness, anxiety, fragmented attention, and civic distrust. The causes are not purely technological, but technology can intensify them by reshaping norms: how we talk to one another, what we reward, what we come to expect from ourselves.

### The trade-offs we make (often without noticing)

Every major technology is a bargain, and the fine print is written in habits. We tend to notice what a tool adds: speed, access, efficiency. We are slower to notice what it displaces: skills, local autonomy, friction that once protected reflection.

Three trade-offs recur across modern systems.

**Convenience vs. agency.**  
Automation removes burdens: navigation removes the need to remember routes; recommendation removes the need to search; AI assistants remove the need to draft, plan, or summarize from scratch. For people with disabilities, overwork, or limited education, these can be liberating supports. Yet a life in which nothing is ever difficult can become a life in which nothing is ever fully *owned*. Agency is not just getting what you want. It is developing the capacity to form wants, revise them, and pursue them through effort that feels like yours. Some frictions are not failures. They are the conditions under which competence, patience, and self-trust grow.

**Connectivity vs. attention and intimacy.**  
Communication tools collapse distance. They can preserve relationships across geography and enable communities that would otherwise be impossible. But they can also produce partial presence: the body is here, the mind is elsewhere, and every quiet moment becomes an opportunity for interruption. Flourishing requires attention—sustained, selective, sometimes protected. Many platforms, however, monetize attention by fragmenting it, rewarding compulsive checking, and privileging content that provokes rapid emotion. The cost is not merely distraction. It is the slow reshaping of what we are able to care about.

**Scale vs. accountability.**  
When systems scale, so do their errors. When decisions are automated, responsibility diffuses. The person affected by a decision—denied a loan, screened out of a job, flagged for “risk,” routed to a worse queue—often has no meaningful path to contest it. Flourishing includes living under conditions one can question and influence. An opaque technological environment is not simply inconvenient; it is politically infantilizing.

If these trade-offs feel abstract, return to the hospital scenario. The scheduling system offers convenience to staff and efficiency to the institution. It scales a set of implicit values—predictability, throughput, risk aversion—across thousands of lives. And when a patient asks why they cannot get an appointment, the answer is no longer a person’s judgment you can appeal to. It is a pattern embedded in a model.

### “Isn’t this just generational panic?”

A fair objection is that every generation believes its new media and machines are uniquely dangerous. People feared the novel, the radio, television, video games, the internet. Society adapted. Why assume this time is different?

The answer should not be melodrama. It should be specificity.

Several features of contemporary AI and digital platforms are structurally different from earlier disruptions:

1. **Speed and reversibility.** A television culture emerged over decades; school systems, families, and laws adjusted slowly. Digital systems update weekly, sometimes hourly. Norms and regulations lag behind an environment that keeps changing shape.

2. **Personalization at scale.** Broadcast media showed the same message to millions. Platform media shows different messages to different people, optimized for their vulnerabilities and desires. The public sphere fractures not just because people disagree, but because they are no longer encountering the same world.

3. **Behavioral feedback loops.** Many systems are not merely presenting information; they are learning from your responses in order to shape your next response. This creates an arms race between human attention and machine-optimized persuasion.

4. **Competition with cognitive labor.** Earlier machines mainly supplemented muscle or extended reach. AI increasingly competes with perception, language, and judgment—the capacities by which people navigate reality and earn social recognition.

These differences do not prove catastrophe. They do show why “we adapted before” is not enough. Adaptation is possible, but it is not automatic—and it is not evenly distributed. The people forced to “adapt” first are often those with the least power: workers displaced by automation, children growing up inside attention markets, citizens targeted by sophisticated propaganda, patients sorted by institutional models they cannot see.

### A global perspective: flourishing also means arrival

Another challenge is that many critiques of modern technology are written from the standpoint of affluent societies that have technology in excess. For billions of people, the urgent question is not whether technology fragments attention but whether it arrives at all. Mobile banking can protect savings from theft and corruption. Telemedicine can reach rural patients. Precision agriculture and weather forecasting can reduce hunger. Satellite connectivity can bring education to places without teachers. It would be parochial, even decadent, to treat “less technology” as an obvious route to flourishing in such contexts.

This point strengthens rather than weakens the power/wisdom framing. In the Global South, the promise of technology is often direct: less preventable suffering, more autonomy, more opportunity. But the risks are also direct: extraction of data without local benefit, dependence on foreign platforms, labor exploitation in supply chains, or the importation of surveillance infrastructures under the banner of development.

The question, globally, is not whether technology is good, but whose ends it serves. If technological capability is power, then development is partly the struggle to ensure that power does not arrive only as someone else’s leverage.

### Flourishing in an age of AI: protecting old goods, cultivating new ones

It is tempting to define flourishing in opposition to AI: authentic human labor, unmediated relationships, pure thought. That purity standard collapses on contact with history. The printing press mediated thought. Schools standardized knowledge. Even language is inherited technology.

A better approach is twofold: protect human capacities that remain central to a good life, and cultivate new forms of excellence that emerge only in partnership with powerful systems.

Four elements matter, but they are not a flat list. They depend on one another.

**1) Epistemic integrity: a world that can be known.**  
If we cannot share a baseline reality, the rest of flourishing becomes fragile. Meaningful agency requires accurate maps of the world. Democratic oversight requires common facts. Relationships require trust.

AI-generated content, deepfakes, and automated persuasion threaten this integrity—not only by spreading falsehoods, but by making people unsure whether anything is true. The endpoint is not gullibility; it is cynicism. When citizens conclude that every image could be fake and every claim could be propaganda, they withdraw into tribes or despair.

Protecting epistemic integrity will require technical measures (provenance standards, authentication, watermarking) and institutional ones (rules for political advertising, liability regimes for certain high-stakes deceptions). It will also require cultural habits: slower journalism, norms that penalize virality without verification, and education that treats media literacy as civic infrastructure.

**2) Meaningful agency: being an author, not merely a user.**  
AI can enhance agency by lowering barriers to expertise—helping someone draft a letter, learn a concept, translate a document, or prototype a business idea. That is real empowerment.

But agency erodes when systems stop being tools and become default governors of choice: when recommendations become destiny; when nudges become invisible steering; when people are trained to consult the model before consulting themselves. Flourishing requires that people retain the ability to set ends, not merely receive optimized means.

This is where new virtues may be required—virtues of *partnership* with AI: knowing when to rely on it and when to resist; how to interrogate outputs; how to preserve one’s own judgment; how to treat a fluent system as fallible. In other words, flourishing may demand not just “critical thinking” in the abstract, but a practiced skill: collaborating with an intelligent tool without surrendering authorship.

**3) Dignified contribution: beyond the wage.**  
Work is not only income. It is structure, mastery, social recognition, and a way of being needed. Automation can remove drudgery and danger; it can also hollow out pathways to competence and belonging.

The strongest counterargument here comes from the post-work tradition, from Aristotle’s *scholē* to Russell’s “In Praise of Idleness” to contemporary advocates of shorter workweeks and universal basic income. They are right about at least two things: much paid labor is pointless or degrading, and leisure can be the space for art, friendship, learning, and civic life. A society that never escapes the necessity of toil is not flourishing; it is surviving.

The problem is not the idea of less work. It is the transition and the distribution. Leisure without community can become isolation. Time without recognition can become invisibility. If automation removes the jobs that offered status and identity while leaving people alone with screens and precariousness, we will not get Aristotle’s leisure; we will get abandonment. Flourishing requires institutions that convert productivity gains into shared security and into real opportunities for contribution—caregiving, mentoring, local governance, craft, art—forms of value that markets often underpay but that lives depend on.

**4) Moral and civic responsibility: systems we can answer for.**  
In the hospital scenario, the most corrosive phrase is: “the model decided.” It tempts everyone to abdicate. Yet the model embodies choices: what counts as success, whose outcomes matter, what trade-offs are acceptable, what errors are tolerable. A flourishing society cannot outsource these choices to opacity.

This implies governance that is more than corporate “ethics boards.” It means clear lines of accountability for high-stakes systems, rights to explanation and appeal where feasible, and democratic oversight of deployments that shape life chances: employment, credit, housing, healthcare, policing, education.

### What we should do: one concrete proposal, and a standard

The temptation at this point is to end with abstractions: regulate more, design better, educate citizens. All true. Also insufficient. The essay’s own argument implies something sharper: when technology becomes infrastructure, we need institutions that can contest it the way we contest other infrastructures.

Here is one concrete proposal that follows directly from the automated-gatekeeper problem:

**Create “Algorithmic Due Process” requirements for high-stakes public and quasi-public systems.**

In domains like healthcare, employment screening, credit, housing allocation, and public benefits, organizations that use AI to make or materially shape decisions would be legally required to provide:

1. **Notice:** clear disclosure that an automated system is involved and what role it plays.
2. **Explanation:** a meaningful account of the factors that drove the decision (not model internals, but actionable reasons).
3. **Appeal:** a human review pathway with authority to override, plus timelines.
4. **Auditability:** routine third-party audits for disparate impact, error rates across groups, and alignment with stated goals.
5. **Procurement transparency:** when public money is involved, model vendors and contracts should be open to scrutiny, including performance claims and known limitations.
6. **Purpose constraints:** restrictions on repurposing data or models beyond the context for which consent and oversight were granted.

This is not a silver bullet. But it converts a moral requirement—living under contestable conditions—into a procedural reality. It also shifts the burden from isolated individuals (“be wiser online”) to systems (“be governable in public”).

Around this proposal, broader principles can be stated more concretely:

- Treat attention, privacy, and autonomy as public goods *because* markets reliably underprice them when revenue depends on surveillance and compulsion.
- Build human infrastructure—education, libraries, public spaces, community institutions—*because* leisure and capability only become flourishing when there are meaningful places to put them.
- Apply subsidiarity where possible—local input into deployments in schools, workplaces, and city services—*because* technology that restructures the field of options must be answerable to those whose options it restructures.
- Pursue global equity not as charity but as stability: technology that serves only wealthy consumers’ appetites while extracting labor and data elsewhere will corrode the legitimacy of the entire system.

### A richer account of technology’s gifts: joy, beauty, wonder

A final honesty is owed to the topic. Not all of technology’s value is defensive—reducing suffering, preventing harm, avoiding manipulation. Technology can also enlarge joy. It can give a teenager in a small town access to music theory and a digital orchestra. It can let a father record his grandmother’s stories in a language that might otherwise disappear. It can make art collaborative across continents. It can put the night sky in your pocket—maps of stars, images from telescopes, the sense of living inside a vast, intelligible universe.

These pleasures matter. They are not mere “entertainment.” Beauty and play are part of flourishing. A critique of technology that cannot speak about wonder will eventually sound like it is arguing for a life of grim virtue. The task is not to purge delight from modern life. It is to prevent our delight from being engineered into dependency, and to ensure that the gains of capability make room for deeper goods rather than crowding them out.

### Conclusion: the question technology forces on us

Return to the hospital gatekeeper. Imagine two futures.

In one, the tool remains opaque. It becomes embedded in every institution. People learn to treat its outputs as fate. The system is efficient. It is also quietly cruel, because no one is responsible in a way that can be reached.

In the other, the same capability exists, but it is surrounded by due process, transparent goals, and avenues for contestation. Clinicians use it as support, not authority. Patients can challenge it. The institution is still efficient, but it is also answerable. The power has been paired—imperfectly, continuously—with wisdom.

This is the real relationship between technology and flourishing: not a ladder we climb, nor a beast we must tame once and for all, but a permanent governance problem. Capability will keep expanding. The question is whether our norms and institutions will expand too—fast enough, concretely enough—to keep human beings from becoming the raw material of someone else’s optimization.

Flourishing in an age of AI will not be achieved by refusing powerful tools, and it will not be achieved by worshiping them. It will be achieved when we insist, in law and in culture, that technology remain a means—serving lives that are intelligible, contestable, and worth wanting. The future is not “more tech” or “less tech.” It is whether our power will be guided by human purposes, or whether human purposes will be quietly rewritten to fit the machines we built.
