# The Conditional Promise of Technology

We live in an age of remarkable technological abundance. The average smartphone possesses more computational power than the machines that sent astronauts to the moon. Artificial intelligence can generate art, diagnose diseases, and hold conversations that feel startlingly human. Biotechnology promises to extend our lives and eliminate hereditary diseases. And yet, amid this unprecedented capability, a curious disquiet persists. Surveys consistently show that rates of anxiety, depression, and loneliness have risen sharply precisely in the societies most saturated with advanced technology. This is not a coincidence, nor is it simply a matter of bad luck or individual failing. It is a signal—a suggestion that the relationship between technological power and human flourishing is far more complex than we often assume.

The central question is not whether technology can enhance human life. It demonstrably can, and has. The agricultural revolution enabled permanent settlements and the rise of civilization. The printing press democratized knowledge and accelerated the spread of ideas. Modern medicine has saved billions of lives and alleviated suffering on a scale previous generations could not have imagined. To deny technology's contributions to human flourishing would be to ignore overwhelming evidence.

But we must first ask what we mean by flourishing—for the answer shapes everything that follows. I take flourishing to involve more than the satisfaction of preferences or the absence of suffering. Drawing on a broadly Aristotelian understanding, I propose that human flourishing requires earned achievement (the satisfaction that comes from mastering something difficult), deep and demanding relationships (not merely the presence of connections but their quality), the capacity for sustained attention (the ability to immerse oneself in complex tasks without distraction), and what we might call epistemic agency—our ability to know how we know what we know, and to take responsibility for our own interpretations of the world. These conditions cannot be reduced to efficiency, convenience, or the absence of pain. They involve struggle, uncertainty, and the exercise of capacities that can only be developed through practice.

With this understanding in place, the more honest observation becomes clear: increasing technological capability does not *necessarily* lead to a better human experience. Technology is not a simple multiplier of well-being. It is something more subtle and more dangerous—a force that reshapes the conditions of human life in ways that may serve some values while undermining others, often in directions we did not intend and may not even notice.

Consider what we have gained and what we have lost in the transition to a digitally mediated existence. We have gained instant access to nearly the sum of human knowledge, the ability to connect with anyone on Earth, and tools for creative expression that once required years of specialized training. We have lost—and this is harder to quantify—the capacity for sustained attention, the experience of boredom that breeds creativity, the specific gravity of a handwritten letter versus the weightlessness of an email, and perhaps most significantly, the uncomfortable but necessary encounter with uncertainty. When every question has an answer a click away, when every moment of waiting can be filled with stimulation, when our devices manage our schedules and remind us to breathe, something in the human capacity for depth and resilience may quietly atrophy.

This is not a nostalgic argument for a return to some imagined pre-technological golden age. Such nostalgia is both romantic and false. Pre-modern life was brutish, short, and filled with suffering that we today can barely imagine. The question is not whether to embrace technology but how to embrace it wisely—and that requires acknowledging the trade-offs we make, often without conscious choice.

The most significant trade-off involves the nature of human agency itself. Each technology we adopt comes embedded with certain assumptions about what matters and how we should live. The architect of a social media platform makes thousands of micro-decisions—about what to show, what to reward, what to bury—that shape not just what we see but how we think and what we desire. We may believe we are using the technology, but the technology is also using us, forming habits of mind and patterns of behavior that are not easily reversed. The philosopher Jacques Ellul warned decades ago that we must distinguish between techniques, which are neutral means, and technique, which is a comprehensive way of thinking that reduces all problems to technical solutions. When we surrender more of our lives to algorithmic curation, we are not merely using a tool; we are entering into a relationship in which our attention, our relationships, and eventually our judgments are shaped by systems whose goals may not align with our own.

This points to a deeper issue: the question of what we mean by human flourishing in the first place. If we define flourishing purely in terms of convenience, efficiency, and the satisfaction of expressed preferences, then technology has indeed delivered. We can order food, find mates, and amuse ourselves with unprecedented ease. But if flourishing involves something more—if it requires struggle, difficulty, the mastery of challenging tasks, the satisfaction of earned achievement, deep and demanding relationships, and the capacity to face mortality and uncertainty with equanimity—then the picture becomes more complicated. Convenience, research suggests, is not a reliable path to meaning. The activities that most contribute to a sense of meaningfulness are often precisely those that are difficult, effortful, and uncertain: learning a skill, raising a child, building something, working through a problem. Technologies that remove friction may also remove the conditions for meaning.

If meaning requires earned achievement, then we must ask what happens when we cease earning even our basic cognitive functions. Each generation of technology tends to automate not just physical tasks but cognitive and emotional ones. We no longer need to remember phone numbers, navigate with maps, or perform mental arithmetic. These may seem like trivial losses, but they add up. When we offload the demands of memory to our devices, we may weaken the capacity for deep recall that underwrites a sense of personal continuity and identity. When we let algorithms curate our information, we may lose the ability to discern quality and think independently. When we delegate difficult emotional labor to therapeutic apps and AI companions, we may diminish our capacity for genuine intimacy and self-understanding. The concern is not that technology makes us stupid—though some evidence suggests it may affect attention and memory—but that it shifts the locus of competence from the individual to the system, creating a form of collective atrophying that is hard to detect because it happens gradually and is masked by the convenience of the moment.

One common objection to this line of argument is that humans have always adapted to new technologies, and that our current anxieties will prove as misplaced as those aroused by the printing press, the telegraph, or television. This objection has merit. Every technological revolution has produced moral panic followed by adaptation. But adaptation is not the same as thriving, and the fact that we can adjust to new conditions does not mean those conditions are good for us. We can adapt to noise, to pollution, to loneliness—but these adaptations are themselves forms of damage. Moreover, the pace and scope of current technological change may exceed anything in human experience. Previous technologies augmented specific human capacities; artificial intelligence threatens to augment or replace the capacity for thought itself. When a large language model can produce a coherent essay or solve a complex problem, what happens to the student's understanding of the material? They may acquire information without acquiring the structural comprehension that writing the essay themselves would have required. This is not merely a matter of convenience or efficiency; it is a qualitative shift in the relationship between knowledge and competence. The printing press democratized access to information; AI democratizes the production of knowledge without requiring the understanding that traditionally accompanied it. The adaptation argument assumes a continuity with the past that the present may not sustain.

A more sophisticated version of this counterargument holds that the problem is not technology but its design and governance—that with the right incentives, we could build technologies that enhance flourishing without the attendant harms. This is the position of those who advocate for "human-centered design," "value-sensitive design," and thoughtful regulation. It is a position I find partially convincing. It is possible to build technologies that respect attention rather than exploit it, that enhance rather than replace human judgment, that create connection rather than isolation. Some technologists are already attempting this. But I am skeptical that market forces alone will produce such outcomes. The economic incentives of the attention economy are powerfully aligned against human well-being, and the track record of self-regulation in the industry is not encouraging. Moreover, even well-designed technologies encounter the fundamental problem that they exist within a broader cultural and economic context that shapes their use in unpredictable ways. A tool designed for connection can become a vector for isolation; a tool designed for information can become a vector for disinformation. The design matters, but it is not sufficient.

One might also argue that the billions of people who voluntarily adopt these technologies are thereby demonstrating their preference for them, and that revealed preferences are the only valid measure of flourishing. But this objection assumes that human choice operates freely in environments engineered to exploit psychological vulnerabilities—variable reward schedules that mimic gambling, infinite scroll that eliminates natural stopping points, notifications designed to trigger dopamine responses. When the very mechanisms that shape our choices are optimized for engagement rather than well-being, we cannot infer flourishing from adoption rates alone. The fact that billions of people use social media does not prove it makes them flourishing; it proves only that it is difficult to resist.

There is another dimension we must acknowledge: the question of who bears the costs of our technological convenience. The servers that store our data are maintained by underpaid workers in the Global South who endure traumatic content so that we need not. The minerals in our devices are extracted in conditions that devastate communities and ecosystems. The "frictionless" experience of the modern internet depends on a vast infrastructure of invisible labor—content moderators, data annotators, warehouse workers—whose own flourishing is sacrificed so that ours may appear seamless. To speak of technology and human flourishing without acknowledging these distributive questions is to speak only of one segment of humanity, and a privileged segment at that.

So where does this leave us? Not in the camp of technological pessimism, which is as simplistic as technological optimism. Not in a call to abandon our devices and return to some prelapsarian state. But in a position of clear-eyed conditionality: technology can contribute to human flourishing, but only if we approach it with intention, critical awareness, and a willingness to make trade-offs that the market will not make for us. This requires cultivating what we might call technological wisdom—the capacity to discern what technologies serve genuinely human ends and what merely simulate that service while eroding the conditions for it. It requires demanding more from those who build and deploy technologies, and accepting that convenience and profit are not adequate measures of value. It requires, finally, reclaiming the authority over how we live—the attention, the time, the relationships, the uncertainty—that makes human flourishing possible.

What would technological wisdom actually look like in practice? It might mean choosing a phone that does not reward constant checking, or deliberately cultivating periods of unstructured time. It might mean accepting that some tasks are better done slowly, that some confusion is generative rather than wasteful, that the point of a hike is not to arrive but to move through space under one's own power. It might mean recognizing that the most meaningful achievements are often the most inefficient, and that a society optimized for convenience may be optimized away from the conditions that make life worth living. The question of what it means to flourish in the age of AI is ultimately a question about what kind of life we want to live and what kind of people we want to become. Technology will not answer this for us. It can only offer us more efficient means toward whatever ends we choose. The ends remain ours to determine—but we must determine them with open eyes, aware that some roads, however convenient, lead to destinations we did not intend and cannot easily escape.

# The Augmented Condition: Technology and the Question of Flourishing

We live in an age that would have seemed miraculous to previous generations. A device in my pocket contains more computational power than the machines that sent astronauts to the moon. With a few taps, I can summon groceries to my door, consult the accumulated knowledge of humanity, or video-chat with someone on the other side of the world. And now, increasingly, I can delegate to artificial systems tasks that once required years of training—a lawyer can generate a brief, an artist can produce an image, a programmer can debug code. The trajectory seems clear: technology expands what humans can do, and therefore, one might conclude, it expands what it means to flourish.

But this reasoning, while understandable, is too quick. The relationship between technological capability and human flourishing is neither straightforward nor guaranteed. Technology can enable flourishing, but it can also undermine it—and often does both at once. The question is not whether technology improves our circumstances, but whether it actually makes our lives better in the ways that matter most. To answer that, we must think carefully about what flourishing actually requires, and then ask whether the technologies we adopt move us toward or away from it.

## The Paradox of Capability

The most common argument for technology's contribution to flourishing points to capability: we can live longer, communicate faster, travel farther, and accomplish more than ever before. This is not trivial. Technologies like antibiotics, clean water systems, and modern transportation have saved billions of lives and extended human possibility in ways that are genuinely admirable. It would be perverse to deny that such advances constitute genuine improvements in the human condition.

Yet capability is not the same as flourishing. One can have the power to do many things while still feeling that life lacks meaning, connection, or purpose. The philosopher Hans Jonas observed that technological power has expanded far faster than our wisdom about how to use it—we can do things long before we understand whether we should. This gap between capability and judgment is not a temporary glitch but a permanent feature of our condition in the technological age.

Consider the smartphone. It is arguably the most consequential technology of the past two decades, and it exemplifies technology's double edge. It has democratized access to information, enabled new forms of creative expression, and kept us connected to people we would otherwise lose track of. But it has also contributed to epidemic levels of anxiety, depression, and attention fragmentation—particularly among young people. We can reach anyone, but we are often more isolated than ever. We have access to infinite information, but we struggle to concentrate long enough to understand anything deeply. The technology did not cause these problems, exactly, but it created conditions that make them far more likely.

This is the paradox of capability: the very features that make a technology powerful often generate trade-offs that are easy to overlook in the enthusiasm of adoption. Convenience comes at the cost of skill. Infinite options can produce paralysis rather than freedom. The ability to communicate with everyone can erode the depth of connection with anyone.

## The Trade-Offs We Don't See

When we adopt new technologies, we typically focus on what we gain. But every adoption also involves a loss, even if that loss is invisible at first. The economist Kenneth Boulding called these "the penalties of the automobile"—the unpriced costs that appear not in our individual decisions but in the social and environmental fabric we share.

Some trade-offs are material: the shift to digital news has devastated the business models that supported investigative journalism, leaving us with more information but arguably less knowledge. The automation of manufacturing has produced cheaper goods while hollowing out communities that depended on meaningful industrial work. These are well-documented and widely debated.

But the more interesting trade-offs are psychological and existential. When we offload cognitive tasks to technology—navigation, memory, calculation, even decision-making—we may gain efficiency but we also lose something. The psychologist Sherry Turkle has documented how the expectation of constant connectivity changes not just how we communicate but how we relate to ourselves. When we can always be reached, we can never fully be present. When we can always look something up, we never quite commit it to memory. These losses are subtle, but they accumulate.

There is also the question of autonomy. Each technology we adopt creates a dependency. We become reliant on the companies that provide our platforms, the infrastructure that supports our tools, and the systems that maintain the knowledge we access. This dependency is not inherently problematic, but it does shift power away from individuals and toward institutions. In an age of AI, this dynamic becomes more pronounced: the systems that increasingly mediate our access to information, employment, and even social connection are controlled by a small number of organizations whose incentives may not align with our flourishing.

## Flourishing in the Age of AI

The arrival of powerful artificial intelligence intensifies these questions dramatically. For the first time, we are building systems that can perform cognitive tasks that were once the exclusive domain of human intelligence—reasoning, creativity, judgment. The implications for human flourishing are profound and contested.

One response is optimism. If AI can handle more of the routine and tedious work that occupies so much of our professional lives, humans might be freed to focus on what is distinctively valuable: relationships, creativity, meaning-making, and the pursuit of wisdom. The economist John Maynard Keynes predicted that technological unemployment would eventually give way to a society of leisure and abundance. Perhaps AI will finally deliver on that promise.

But this optimism rests on an assumption that deserves scrutiny: that human flourishing depends primarily on what we consume and produce, rather than on what we do and who we are. The philosopher Charles Taylor has argued that modern society suffers from a "meaning crisis"—a widespread sense that life lacks significance, purpose, or coherence. This is not primarily a material problem. People in wealthy, technologically advanced societies are not obviously happier or more fulfilled than those in simpler circumstances. The question, then, is not whether AI will make us more productive, but whether it will help us live lives we experience as meaningful.

Here, the evidence is more mixed. AI can certainly assist in creative and intellectual pursuits, and many people find tools like large language models genuinely useful for thinking through problems and generating ideas. But there is also a risk that outsourcing cognition to AI erodes the very capacities that give work its meaning. If a composer uses AI to generate music, is the result still an expression of their creative vision? If a student uses AI to write essays, do they develop the capacity for rigorous thinking? The technology itself is neutral, but its deployment in contexts of education, work, and creative work has consequences for human development that are not trivial.

More fundamentally, AI challenges the assumption that human worth is tied to what we can do. If machines can match or exceed human performance across a widening range of tasks, what remains distinctively valuable about being human? The answer, I think, is not in our cognitive abilities but in our relationality—our capacity for empathy, for moral responsibility, for love. These are not computational capacities. They emerge from our embodiment, our vulnerability, and our immersion in webs of meaning and relationship that no algorithm can replicate. If we want to flourish in the age of AI, we must cultivate these distinctly human capacities, not compete with machines on their terms.

## A Conditional Relationship

What should we conclude? Not that technology is bad, certainly, but that the relationship between technology and human flourishing is conditional, not causal. Technology can enable flourishing, but it can also undermine it, and the outcome depends on the wisdom with which we adopt and deploy it.

This means that the question of technology is ultimately a question about values. What do we want life to be about? What do we want our relationships to look like? What do we consider meaningful work? These are not questions that technology can answer for us. They are questions that each generation must answer for itself, using whatever tools are available.

The challenge of our time is not to resist technology—that is neither possible nor desirable—but to remain thoughtful about its integration into our lives. This requires cultivating what the philosopher Albert Borgmann called "device paradigm": the discipline to use technology intentionally rather than habitually, to preserve spaces of unmediated experience, and to maintain the skills and relationships that give life its depth.

We are not passive recipients of technological change. We are participants in a collective project of shaping what technology means for human life. That project requires not just innovation but reflection—not just asking what we can do, but what we should do, and what we want to become. In the end, the question of technology is the question of what kind of life we want to live.

This gap between capability and judgment is not a temporary glitch but a permanent feature of our condition in the technological age.

Consider the smartphone. It is arguably the most consequential technology of the past two decades, and it exemplifies technology's double edge. It has democratized access to information, enabled new forms of creative expression, and kept us connected to people we would otherwise lose track of. But it has also contributed to epidemic levels of anxiety, depression, and attention fragmentation—particularly among young people. We can reach anyone, but we are often more isolated than ever. We have access to infinite information, but we struggle to concentrate long enough to understand anything deeply.

Or consider a more subtle example: GPS navigation. The technology is genuinely useful—we no longer get lost, we always arrive at our destination efficiently. But something interesting happens to our sense of space when we stop building cognitive maps in our minds. Studies have shown that heavy GPS users exhibit reduced activity in the hippocampus, the brain region associated with spatial memory. We gain efficiency but lose the ability to navigate on our own, to build mental models of the world, to feel a sense of place. The technology does not just get us there; it changes the architecture of how we think. This is the paradox of capability: the very features that make a technology powerful often generate trade-offs that are easy to overlook in the enthusiasm of adoption.

## The Trade-Offs We Don't See

When we adopt new technologies, we typically focus on what we gain. But every adoption also involves a loss, even if that loss is invisible at first. The economist Kenneth Boulding called these "the penalties of the automobile"—the unpriced costs that appear not in our individual decisions but in the social and environmental fabric we share.

Some trade-offs are material: the shift to digital news has devastated the business models that supported investigative journalism, leaving us with more information but arguably less knowledge. The automation of manufacturing has produced cheaper goods while hollowing out communities that depended on meaningful industrial work. These are well-documented and widely debated.

But the more interesting trade-offs are psychological and existential. When we offload cognitive tasks to technology—navigation, memory, calculation, even decision-making—we may gain efficiency but we also lose something. The psychologist Sherry Turkle has documented how the expectation of constant connectivity changes not just how we communicate but how we relate to ourselves. When we can always be reached, we can never fully be present. When we can always look something up, we never quite commit it to memory. These losses are subtle, but they accumulate.

There is also the question of autonomy. Each technology we adopt creates a dependency. We become reliant on the companies that provide our platforms, the infrastructure that supports our tools, and the systems that maintain the knowledge we access. This dependency is not inherently problematic, but it does shift power away from individuals and toward institutions. In an age of AI, this dynamic becomes more pronounced: the systems that increasingly mediate our access to information, employment, and even social connection are controlled by a small number of organizations whose incentives may not align with our flourishing.

## Flourishing in the Age of AI

The arrival of powerful artificial intelligence intensifies these questions dramatically. For the first time, we are building systems that can perform cognitive tasks that were once the exclusive domain of human intelligence—reasoning, creativity, judgment. The implications for human flourishing are profound and contested.

One response is optimism. If AI can handle more of the routine and tedious work that occupies so much of our professional lives, humans might be freed to focus on what is distinctively valuable: relationships, creativity, meaning-making, and the pursuit of wisdom. The economist John Maynard Keynes predicted in 1930 that technological unemployment would eventually give way to a society of leisure and abundance. Surely, the argument goes, AI will finally deliver on that promise.

But this optimism rests on an assumption that deserves scrutiny: that human flourishing depends primarily on what we consume and produce, rather than on what we do and who we are. The historical record is not encouraging. Keynes's prediction has not come to pass—not because technology failed to increase productivity, but because abundance generated its own demands. We work more hours than medieval peasants, not less. The "leisure society" never arrived, because each technological gain seemed to create new needs, new anxieties, new competitions. The question, then, is not whether AI will make us more productive, but whether it will help us live lives we experience as meaningful.

Here, the evidence is more mixed. AI can certainly assist in creative and intellectual pursuits, and many people find tools like large language models genuinely useful for thinking through problems and generating ideas. But there is also a risk that outsourcing cognition to AI erodes the very capacities that give work its meaning. If a composer uses AI to generate music, is the result still an expression of their creative vision? If a student uses AI to write essays, do they develop the capacity for rigorous thinking?

More fundamentally, AI poses a challenge to the assumption that human worth is tied to what we can do. If machines can match or exceed human performance across a widening range of tasks, what remains distinctively valuable about being human? The answer, I think, is not in our cognitive abilities but in our relationality—our capacity for empathy, for moral responsibility, for love. These are not computational capacities. They emerge from our embodiment, our vulnerability, and our immersion in webs of meaning and relationship that no algorithm can replicate.

There is also the alignment problem to consider. Even if AI systems become extraordinarily capable, how do we ensure their goals remain aligned with human flourishing? A system optimized for efficiency may optimize for efficiency even when efficiency conflicts with meaning. We may get what we asked for but not what we actually need. This is not science fiction; it is a design challenge that AI researchers are already grappling with. The technology itself is neutral, but its deployment in contexts of education and work risks eroding the very human capacities it seeks to augment.

## A Conditional Relationship

What should we conclude? Not that technology is bad, certainly, but that the relationship between technology and human flourishing is conditional, not causal. Technology can enable flourishing, but it can also undermine it, and the outcome depends on the wisdom with which we adopt and deploy it.

This means that the question of technology is ultimately a question about values. What do we want life to be about? What do we want our relationships to look like? What do we consider meaningful work? These are not questions that technology can answer for us. They are questions that each generation must answer for itself, using whatever tools are available.

The challenge of our time is not to resist technology—that is neither possible nor desirable—but to remain thoughtful about its integration into our lives. This requires resisting what the philosopher Albert Borgmann called the "device paradigm"—the tendency to view the world merely as a resource to be optimized. Instead, we must cultivate what Borgmann termed "focal practices": activities that demand our full engagement and ground us in the physical world—playing music, preparing a meal, walking through a forest without a phone. These are not technological challenges; they are human ones.

We are not passive recipients of technological change. We are participants in a collective project of shaping what technology means for human life. That project requires not just innovation but reflection—not just asking what we can do, but what we should do, and what we want to become. If we want to flourish in the age of AI, we must cultivate the distinctly human capacities that no machine can replicate: the capacity to be present, to love, to choose the good over the efficient. In the end, the question of technology is the question of what kind of life we want to live.

What should we conclude? Not that technology is bad—that is neither true nor useful. But we can develop criteria for evaluating whether a particular technology enables or undermines flourishing. I would propose three tests:

First, does the technology enhance or diminish human agency? Technologies that automate decisions we should be making for ourselves—about what to believe, how to spend our time, what to value—undermine the capacity for autonomous life that is central to flourishing.

Second, does the technology create or destroy meaningful work? Work is not merely a means to income; it is a primary way that most people find purpose, develop skills, and contribute to communities. Technologies that eliminate meaningful work without replacing it with alternatives that provide similar benefits are suspect.

Third, does the technology strengthen or weaken real-world relationships? Human beings are inherently social, and flourishing requires deep connections with others. Technologies that substitute shallow online interactions for face-to-face relationships, or that fragment attention in ways that prevent genuine presence, are working against flourishing.

The challenge of our time is not to resist technology—that is neither possible nor desirable—but to remain thoughtful about its integration into our lives. This requires cultivating what the philosopher Albert Borgmann called "device paradigm": the discipline to use technology intentionally rather than habitually, to preserve spaces of unmediated experience, and to maintain the skills and relationships that give life its depth.

These are not technological solutions but social ones—and they may matter more than any feature we could add to a device.

Third, we need to cultivate practices of digital self-regulation—not as moralizing about individual failure, but as skills that we teach and support. Digital sabbaths, screen-free meals, attention training through contemplative practices. These are not solutions to the structural problems, but they can help us preserve the capacities that technology threatens to erode.

This is the paradox of capability: the very features that make a technology powerful often generate trade-offs that are easy to overlook in the enthusiasm of adoption. Convenience comes at the cost of skill. Infinite options can produce paralysis rather than freedom. The ability to communicate with everyone can erode the depth of connection with anyone.

## The Trade-Offs We Don't See

When we adopt new technologies, we typically focus on what we gain. But every adoption also involves a loss, even if that loss is invisible at first. The economist Kenneth Boulding called these "the penalties of the automobile"—the unpriced costs that appear not in our individual decisions but in the social and environmental fabric we share.

Some trade-offs are material: the shift to digital news has devastated the business models that supported investigative journalism, leaving us with more information but arguably less knowledge. The automation of manufacturing has produced cheaper goods while hollowing out communities that depended on meaningful industrial work. These are well-documented and widely debated.

But the more interesting trade-offs are psychological and existential. When we offload cognitive tasks to technology—navigation, memory, calculation, even decision-making—we may gain efficiency but we also lose something. The psychologist Sherry Turkle has documented how the expectation of constant connectivity changes not just how we communicate but how we relate to ourselves. When we can always be reached, we can never fully be present. When we can always look something up, we never quite commit it to memory. These losses are subtle, but they accumulate.

There is also the question of autonomy. Each technology we adopt creates a dependency. We become reliant on the companies that provide our platforms, the infrastructure that supports our tools, and the systems that maintain the knowledge we access. This dependency is not inherently problematic, but it does shift power away from individuals and toward institutions. In an age of AI, this dynamic becomes more pronounced: the systems that increasingly mediate our access to information, employment, and even social connection are controlled by a small number of organizations whose incentives may not align with our flourishing.

It is worth noting, however, that this analysis risks reflecting the concerns of already-affluent societies. For billions of people in the developing world, technology is not primarily a source of psychological trade-offs but a material lifeline. Mobile banking has brought financial services to communities without branch networks. Agricultural data delivered by simple phones has helped farmers increase yields and escape poverty. Health workers use technology to deliver vaccines to remote villages. For those for whom survival itself is at stake, the question of whether technology enables flourishing is less ambiguous—capability and well-being are more directly linked. Any honest account of technology's relationship to human flourishing must acknowledge this global dimension, even as we focus on the more complex challenges facing technologically saturated societies.

## Flourishing in the Age of AI

The arrival of powerful artificial intelligence intensifies these questions dramatically. For the first time, we are building systems that can perform cognitive tasks that were once the exclusive domain of human intelligence—reasoning, creativity, judgment. The implications for human flourishing are profound and contested.

One response is optimism. If AI can handle more of the routine and tedious work that occupies so much of our professional lives, humans might be freed to focus on what is distinctively valuable: relationships, creativity, meaning-making, and the pursuit of wisdom. The economist John Maynard Keynes predicted that technological unemployment would eventually give way to a society of leisure and abundance. Perhaps AI will finally deliver on that promise.

There is a more contemporary version of this optimism: the idea that AI will create entirely new categories of work that require uniquely human skills—prompt engineering, AI ethics oversight, human-machine collaboration design. On this view, we need not fear obsolescence because human creativity and judgment will remain essential, even as the specific nature of work evolves.

But this optimism rests on an assumption that deserves scrutiny: that human flourishing depends primarily on what we consume and produce, rather than on what we do and who we are. The philosopher Charles Taylor has argued that modern society suffers from a "meaning crisis"—a widespread sense that life lacks significance, purpose, or coherence. This is not primarily a material problem. People in wealthy, technologically advanced societies are not obviously happier or more fulfilled than those in simpler circumstances. The question, then, is not whether AI will make us more productive, but whether it will help us live lives we experience as meaningful.

Here, the evidence is more mixed. AI can certainly assist in creative and intellectual pursuits, and many people find tools like large language models genuinely useful for thinking through problems and generating ideas. But there is also a risk that outsourcing cognition to AI erodes the very capacities that give work its meaning. If a composer uses AI to generate music, is the result still an expression of their creative vision? If a student uses AI to write essays, do they develop the capacity for rigorous thinking? The technology itself is neutral, but its deployment in contexts of education, work, and creative work has fundamental consequences for human development.

More fundamentally, AI challenges the assumption that human worth is tied to what we can do. If machines can match or exceed human performance across a widening range of tasks, what remains distinctively valuable about being human? The answer, I think, is not in our cognitive abilities but in our relationality—our capacity for empathy, for moral responsibility, for love. These are not computational capacities. They emerge from our embodiment, our vulnerability, and our immersion in webs of meaning and relationship that no algorithm can replicate. If we want to flourish in the age of AI, we must cultivate these distinctly human capacities, not compete with machines on their terms.

## A Conditional Relationship

What should we conclude? Not that technology is bad, certainly, but that the relationship between technology and human flourishing is conditional, not causal. Technology can enable flourishing, but it can also undermine it, and the outcome depends on the wisdom with which we adopt and deploy it.

This means that the question of technology is ultimately a question about values. What do we want life to be about? What do we want our relationships to look like? What do we consider meaningful work? These are not questions that technology can answer for us. They are questions that each generation must answer for itself, using whatever tools are available.

The challenge of our time is not to resist technology—that is neither possible nor desirable—but to remain thoughtful about its integration into our lives. This requires cultivating what the philosopher Albert Borgmann called the "device paradigm": the discipline to use technology intentionally rather than habitually, to preserve spaces of unmediated experience, and to maintain the skills and relationships that give life its depth. In practice, this might mean periodically disconnecting—a digital sabbath that restores the capacity for solitary reflection, or the deliberate choice to navigate without GPS so we retain our sense of direction. It might mean resisting the efficiency of voice memos and instead committing ideas to memory, preserving the cognitive discipline that deepens understanding. It might mean choosing, at least sometimes, to be unreachable.

If we fail to cultivate this wisdom, we risk achieving unprecedented capability while simultaneously engineering our own existential emptiness—a life of remarkable convenience but diminished depth, where we have outsourced so much of what makes us human that we forget what we have lost. The stakes of uncritical adoption are not trivial; they concern nothing less than the character of human flourishing itself.

We are not passive recipients of technological change. We are participants in a collective project of shaping what technology means for human life. That project requires not just innovation but reflection—not just asking what we can do, but what we should do, and what we want to become. In the end, the question of technology is the question of what kind of life we want to live.

Technology can enable flourishing, but it can also undermine it—and often does both at once.

To see why, we need to be clear about what flourishing actually requires. The concept has ancient roots: Aristotle called it *eudaimonia*, roughly translated as human flourishing or a life lived well. Unlike pleasure or mere satisfaction, eudaimonia is not a feeling but an achievement—a condition of living in which a person realizes their capacities, engages in meaningful relationships, and acts in ways that they themselves endorse as worthy.

Contemporary psychologists have refined this picture. Flourishing involves at least three elements that no technology can directly provide: relationships that involve genuine mutual recognition, mastery over domains that demand effort and skill, and a sense of purpose that connects daily activities to something larger than oneself. These are not commodities to be delivered but capacities to be cultivated. And they are, crucially, relational—they emerge not from what we consume or produce, but from how we spend our attention and what we become through practice.

This matters because it reveals the limit of the capability argument. We can live longer, communicate faster, and accomplish more than ever before. But none of these gains automatically produces relationships, mastery, or purpose. They might, in the right conditions—but they might just as easily crowd them out.

The most common argument for technology's contribution to flourishing points to capability: we can do more, therefore we flourish more. This is not trivial. This gap between capability and judgment is not a temporary glitch but a permanent feature of our condition in the technological age.

It has democratized access to information, enabled new forms of creative expression, and kept us connected to people we would otherwise lose track of. But it has also contributed to epidemic levels of anxiety, depression, and attention fragmentation—particularly among young people. We can reach anyone, but we are often more isolated than ever. We have access to infinite information, but we struggle to concentrate long enough to understand anything deeply.

Or consider GPS navigation. We gain route efficiency but lose spatial awareness and the serendipity of getting lost—of stumbling upon an unexpected cafe, of learning to read a paper map in an unfamiliar city. The technology does not force these losses, but it makes them almost inevitable. When the path is always provided, the capacity to find one's own way atrophies.

This is the paradox of capability: the very features that make a technology powerful often generate trade-offs that are easy to overlook in the enthusiasm of adoption. One might argue that even if technology creates psychological costs, the net welfare gains—longer lives, less physical suffering, more material comfort—still justify it. A person might live longer, eat better, and communicate more efficiently while still experiencing life as shallow, disconnected, and pointless. The question is not whether technology improves our circumstances but whether it makes our lives feel meaningful—and on this question, the evidence is far less encouraging. # The Fragile Gift: Technology and the Question of Human Flourishing

We live in an age of extraordinary technological capability. Within a single generation, we have witnessed the internet transform how we communicate, access information, and conduct nearly every aspect of daily life. Artificial intelligence now composes music, writes essays, and diagnoses diseases. Automation promises to reshape labor in ways we are only beginning to understand. These developments prompt a question that is both ancient and urgently new: does increasing technological capability necessarily lead to a better human experience?

The honest answer is more complicated than either the techno-optimists or the technology skeptics would have us believe. Technology is not a means to flourishing in any straightforward sense, nor is it inherently opposed to human flourishing. What matters—and what we far too often fail to examine—is the relationship we cultivate with our tools, and more fundamentally, what we understand flourishing to be in the first place.

**The Genuine Promise**

It would be foolish to deny that technology has dramatically expanded what human beings can achieve. Medical technologies have eradicated diseases that plagued our ancestors for millennia and extended average life expectancy by decades. Agricultural innovations have lifted billions out of subsistence poverty. Communication technologies allow a farmer in rural India to access the same knowledge as a professor at Oxford. These are not trivial achievements; they represent genuine expansions of human capability and the reduction of profound suffering.

Consider what technology has made possible for those with disabilities: cochlear implants restore hearing, prosthetic limbs restore mobility, and screen readers grant access to the written word to those who cannot see. Technology, in these contexts, does not merely entertain or convenience—it restores capacities that many would consider essential to a fully human life. To dismiss such advances as irrelevant to flourishing would be to define human flourishing so narrowly that it becomes almost contemptible.

Moreover, technology has enriched human life in ways that are easy to overlook when we focus on the latest anxieties. The ability to preserve and share music, art, and literature across continents and generations; the capacity to connect with loved ones across vast distances; the tools that allow humans to understand the universe at scales both cosmic and subatomic—these represent genuine expansions of human experience. There is something admirable and human about using our intelligence to extend our reach, to solve problems, to alleviate suffering.

**The Costs We Underestimate**

Yet the relationship between technological capability and human flourishing is not simply additive. Every technology involves trade-offs, and these trade-offs are often invisible until the costs have already accumulated. We tend to evaluate new technologies in terms of what they add to our lives while systematically underestimating what they displace.

The smartphone offers a useful example. It has genuinely expanded human capability—anyone who has used a maps application to navigate an unfamiliar city or accessed emergency services during a crisis has benefited from these devices. Yet we have also witnessed the emergence of what some have called a "attention economy," in which technology companies deliberately design their products to capture and hold our attention through variable reward mechanisms that exploit fundamental aspects of human psychology. The result has been a widespread erosion of the capacity for sustained attention, for boredom, for the kind of idle contemplation that historically preceded some of our deepest insights and most meaningful experiences.

We should be cautious about attributing too much to technology alone—human beings have always found ways to distract themselves. But there is evidence that the specific affordances of digital technologies are changing not just what we do but how our minds work. The shift from deep reading to skimming, from focused work to constant task-switching, from conversation to communication—these are not merely changes in habit but potentially changes in cognitive architecture. Whether these changes represent genuine losses is a question we should take seriously rather than dismiss as nostalgic hand-wringing.

There are also costs that operate at the level of community and social structure. The decline of institutions that once served as nodes of human connection—religious communities, labor unions, neighborhood associations, extended families living in proximity—has coincided with the rise of technologies that promised to connect us. It would be too simple to blame technology for these shifts, but it would be equally naive to imagine they are unrelated. Human beings are social creatures, and flourishing has always depended in part on belonging, on being known, on participating in communities that transcend the individual. We should be honest about what we may be losing as we replace face-to-face interaction with screen-mediated connection.

**The Question of Flourishing**

To evaluate technology's relationship to human flourishing, we need some account of what flourishing actually means. This is, of course, one of the most contested questions in philosophy, and I cannot resolve it here. But we can note that flourishing involves more than mere preference satisfaction or the accumulation of capabilities. Most accounts include elements like meaningful relationships, a sense of purpose, moral development, intellectual and aesthetic cultivation, and the capacity for authentic agency—the ability to shape one's own life according to one's own values rather than simply responding to stimuli.

This points to something crucial: flourishing is not merely about having more options or greater efficiency. It is about the quality of our experiences, the depth of our connections, and our capacity to live in accordance with what we genuinely value. And here is where technology's relationship to flourishing becomes genuinely complex, because technology can simultaneously expand our options while undermining the conditions that make choices meaningful.

Consider the phenomenon of the "paradox of choice." Psychological research suggests that beyond a certain point, increasing options does not increase satisfaction but decreases it—partly because of the effort required to evaluate choices, partly because of the regret that follows from imperfect decisions, and partly because abundance can trivialise what once seemed significant. If this research is even partially correct, then the technological expansion of possibility does not automatically translate into better lives.

There is also the question of what we might call "flourishing-envy"—the endless comparison with others that social media makes so easy, the constant awareness of experiences we are not having, the curated highlight reels that make our own lives seem inadequate. # The Fragile Gift: Technology and the Question of Human Flourishing

We live in an age of extraordinary technological capability. Within a single generation, the internet has transformed how we communicate, access information, and conduct daily life. Technology is not a means to flourishing in any straightforward sense, nor is it inherently opposed to it. What matters—and what we far too often fail to examine—is the relationship we cultivate with our tools, and fundamentally, what we understand flourishing to mean.

Medical technologies have eradicated diseases that plagued our ancestors for millennia and extended average life expectancy by decades. Agricultural innovations have lifted billions out of subsistence poverty. Communication technologies allow a farmer in rural India to access the same knowledge as a professor at Oxford. These are not trivial achievements; they represent genuine expansions of human capability and the reduction of profound suffering.

Consider what technology has made possible for those with disabilities: cochlear implants restore hearing, prosthetic limbs restore mobility, and screen readers grant access to the written word to those who cannot see. Technology, in these contexts, does not merely entertain or convenience—it restores capacities many would consider essential to a fully human life. To dismiss such advances as irrelevant to flourishing would be to define human flourishing so narrowly that it becomes almost contemptible.

Technology has also enriched human life in ways we easily overlook when focusing on the latest anxieties. The ability to preserve and share music, art, and literature across continents and generations, to connect with loved ones across vast distances, to understand the universe at scales both cosmic and subatomic—these represent genuine expansions of human experience. There is something admirable and human about using our intelligence to extend our reach, to solve problems, to alleviate suffering.

Yet the relationship between technological capability and human flourishing is not simply additive. Every technology involves trade-offs, and these trade-offs are often invisible until costs have already accumulated. We tend to evaluate new technologies in terms of what they add to our lives while systematically underestimating what they displace.

# The Fragile Gift: Technology and the Question of Human Flourishing

We live in an age of extraordinary technological capability. Within a single generation, we have witnessed the internet transform how we communicate, access information, and conduct nearly every aspect of daily life. Artificial intelligence now composes music, writes essays, and diagnoses diseases. Automation promises to reshape labor in ways we are only beginning to understand. These developments prompt a question that is both ancient and urgently new: does increasing technological capability necessarily lead to a better human experience?

The honest answer is more complicated than either the techno-optimists or the technology skeptics would have us believe. Technology is not a means to flourishing in any straightforward sense, nor is it inherently opposed to human flourishing. What matters—and what we far too often fail to examine—is the relationship we cultivate with our tools, and more fundamentally, what we understand flourishing to be in the first place. Indeed, here lies a deeper challenge: technology may not merely serve our conception of flourishing but actively shape that conception itself, subtly redefining what we even mean by a good life.

**The Genuine Promise**

It would be foolish to deny that technology has dramatically expanded what human beings can achieve. Medical technologies have eradicated diseases that plagued our ancestors for millennia and extended average life expectancy by decades. Agricultural innovations have lifted billions out of subsistence poverty. Communication technologies allow a farmer in rural India to access the same knowledge as a professor at Oxford. These are not trivial achievements; they represent genuine expansions of human capability and the reduction of profound suffering.

Consider what technology has made possible for those with disabilities: cochlear implants restore hearing, prosthetic limbs restore mobility, and screen readers grant access to the written word to those who cannot see. Technology, in these contexts, does not merely entertain or convenience—it restores capacities that many would consider essential to a fully human life. To dismiss such advances as irrelevant to flourishing would be to define human flourishing so narrowly that it becomes almost contemptible.

Moreover, technology has enriched human life in ways that are easy to overlook when we focus on the latest anxieties. The ability to preserve and share music, art, and literature across continents and generations; the capacity to connect with loved ones across vast distances; the tools that allow humans to understand the universe at scales both cosmic and subatomic—these represent genuine expansions of human experience. There is something admirable and deeply human about using our intelligence to extend our reach, to solve problems, to alleviate suffering.

**The Costs We Underestimate**

Yet the relationship between technological capability and human flourishing is not simply additive. Every technology involves trade-offs, and these trade-offs are often invisible until the costs have already accumulated. We tend to evaluate new technologies in terms of what they add to our lives while systematically underestimating what they displace.

The smartphone offers a useful example. It has genuinely expanded human capability—anyone who has used a maps application to navigate an unfamiliar city or accessed emergency services during a crisis has benefited from these devices. Yet we have also witnessed the emergence of what some have called an "attention economy," in which technology companies deliberately design their products to capture and hold our attention through variable reward mechanisms that exploit fundamental aspects of human psychology. The result has been a widespread erosion of the capacity for sustained attention, for boredom, for the kind of idle contemplation that historically preceded some of our deepest insights and most meaningful experiences.

We should be cautious about attributing too much to technology alone—human beings have always found ways to distract themselves. But the specific affordances of digital technologies are changing not just what we do but how our minds work. The shift from deep reading to skimming, from focused work to constant task-switching, from conversation to communication—these are not merely changes in habit but potentially changes in cognitive architecture. Whether these changes represent genuine losses is a question we should take seriously rather than dismiss as nostalgic hand-wringing.

There are also costs that operate at the level of community and social structure. The decline of institutions that once served as nodes of human connection—religious communities, labor unions, neighborhood associations, extended families living in proximity—has coincided with the rise of technologies that promised to connect us. It would be too simple to blame technology for these shifts, but it would be equally naive to imagine they are unrelated. Human beings are social creatures, and flourishing has always depended in part on belonging, on being known, on participating in communities that transcend the individual. We should be honest about what we may be losing as we replace face-to-face interaction with screen-mediated connection.

**The Question of Flourishing**

To evaluate technology's relationship to human flourishing, we need some account of what flourishing actually means. This is, of course, one of the most contested questions in philosophy, and I cannot resolve it here. But we can note that flourishing involves more than mere preference satisfaction or the accumulation of capabilities. Most accounts include elements like meaningful relationships, a sense of purpose, moral development, intellectual and aesthetic cultivation, and the capacity for authentic agency—the ability to shape one's own life according to one's own values rather than simply responding to stimuli.

This points to something crucial: flourishing is not merely about having more options or greater efficiency. It is about the quality of our experiences, the depth of our connections, and our capacity to live in accordance with what we genuinely value. And here is where technology's relationship to flourishing becomes genuinely complex, because technology can simultaneously expand our options while undermining the conditions that make choices meaningful.

Modern culture tends to equate flourishing with ease—the removal of friction, the minimization of effort, the optimization of pleasure. Technology, in this framing, becomes the great enabler of a frictionless life. But this conception deserves scrutiny. Consider what we lose when we eliminate difficulty: the satisfaction of mastering a challenging skill, the depth of relationships forged through sustained effort, the character that forms through overcoming obstacles. The philosopher Josef Pieper argued that leisure—the capacity for contemplation and festivity—is the basis of culture, but leisure is not the same as mere idleness or the passive consumption of entertainment. True flourishing may require precisely the kind of friction that technology aims to remove.

This insight reveals a paradox at the heart of technological progress. We adopt tools to make life easier, but ease itself may undermine the conditions for a meaningful life. The capacity for sustained attention, for delayed gratification, for tolerating the discomfort of uncertainty—these are not quirks to be engineered away but essential ingredients of human flourishing that technology may be eroding.

Consider the phenomenon of the "paradox of choice." Psychological research suggests that beyond a certain point, increasing options does not increase satisfaction but decreases it—partly because of the effort required to evaluate choices, partly because of the regret that follows from imperfect decisions, and partly because abundance can trivialize what once seemed significant. If this research is even partially correct, then the technological expansion of possibility does not automatically translate into better lives.

There is also the question of what we might call "flourishing-envy"—the endless comparison with others that social media makes so easy, the constant awareness of experiences we are not having, the curated highlight reels that make our own lives seem inadequate. Technology does not create human jealousy or dissatisfaction, but it has amplified these tendencies in ways that may make authentic contentment more difficult to achieve.

**AI, Automation, and the Future of Flourishing**

The emergence of artificial intelligence and automation raises these questions in an acute form. On one hand, AI has the potential to liberate human beings from repetitive, mind-numbing labor, creating space for more creative, relational, and meaningful work. If successful, this could represent the most significant expansion of human flourishing in history.

Yet we must be honest about the uncertainties and the more subtle dangers. The transition to an automated economy could create massive dislocation and inequality, leaving many without meaningful work or the income that work provides. Even beyond the economic disruption lies a deeper philosophical challenge: the question of what people will do with their time if machines can perform most productive labor has no easy answer. Work has historically provided not just income but structure, purpose, community, and a sense of contribution. Replacing it requires not merely economic planning but a cultural and philosophical reimagining of what makes life meaningful.

More troubling still is what we might call the "displacement of agency." As AI systems become increasingly sophisticated at making decisions—from what we watch to where we go to how we write—they risk atrophying the very capacities that give human life its distinctive value. The philosopher Albert Borgmann spoke of "the device paradigm," in which technology withdraws from our attention, leaving us with commodities rather than engagements. If AI serves as what some have called an "exocortex"—an external brain that thinks for us—we may lose the ability to think for ourselves, to exercise judgment, to struggle with difficult problems.

This connects to a deeper question about process versus product. When I write these words, I experience the struggle of finding the right phrase, the satisfaction of revision, the gradual emergence of an argument. If an AI could generate a superior essay in a fraction of a second, something would be lost—not in the quality of the output, but in the human activity itself. The process of creation, of effort, of overcoming resistance, may be where much of human flourishing resides. We cannot simply dismiss the fear that AI makes human effort obsolete without examining what that effort has always meant.

Consider the counterargument: if AI makes life easier, isn't that precisely the definition of flourishing? The answer depends on what we think flourishing actually is. If it is merely the accumulation of pleasant experiences or the satisfaction of preferences, then perhaps ease is all that matters. But if flourishing involves the exercise of capacities, the development of character, the engagement with difficulty—then the removal of effort may be its own kind of poverty. The child who is never allowed to struggle with a math problem never experiences the satisfaction of mastery. The adult who outsources every difficult decision never develops practical wisdom. We should be slow to accept that ease is the highest good.

**Toward Wisdom**

The answer to the question of technology and flourishing is not to reject technology—that is neither possible nor desirable—but to cultivate a wiser relationship with our tools. This requires several things we currently lack.

First, it requires that we think more carefully about what we are trying to achieve. What is flourishing? What do we want from life? These are questions that technology cannot answer, and they are questions we must answer before we can intelligently evaluate whether any particular technology serves or undermines our goals. Moreover, we must remain alert to the possibility that our tools are shaping these questions in ways we do not recognize.

Second, it requires what we might call technological humility—the recognition that we cannot fully foresee the consequences of the tools we create. The inventors of social media did not set out to create a machine for political polarization and mental health crisis; they envisioned connection and community. The lesson is not that we should stop innovating but that we should approach new technologies with appropriate caution and a willingness to course-correct when harms become evident.

Third, it requires that we attend to what technology displaces. When we adopt a new tool, we should ask not only what it adds but what it might be crowding out. The capacity for sustained attention, for boredom, for reflection, for face-to-face connection—these are not automatic byproducts of technological progress. They must be cultivated, protected, and sometimes deliberately preserved against the tendency of efficiency to eliminate them.

Fourth, and perhaps most concretely, we might recognize that there are domains where efficiency should not be the primary goal. Parenting, friendship, prayer, the appreciation of nature, the experience of art—these are activities whose value lies partly in their difficulty, their slowness, their resistance to optimization. Technological humility might mean refusing to bring efficiency-maximizing tools into these spaces, not because technology is evil, but because some parts of life should remain beyond its reach.

Technology is a remarkable gift, but like all gifts, its value depends on how we receive it. The metaphor of the gift is apt: a gift can be received poorly, hoarded anxiously, or used in ways that wound the giver. We have given ourselves remarkable tools, and now we must learn to receive them wisely. Increasing technological capability does not automatically lead to a better human experience, but it can—under the right conditions, with the right intentions, and accompanied by wisdom about what truly matters. The challenge of our age is not to resist technology or to embrace it uncritically, but to become more deliberate about the relationship we cultivate with the powerful tools we have created. In doing so, we may discover that the question of flourishing was always, at its heart, a question about what kind of life we want to live—and that technology, for all its power, remains a means to an end we must define for ourselves. The gift is fragile; we must learn to be worthy of it.

# The Fragile Gift: Technology and the Question of Human Flourishing

What does it mean to live well? It is a question that has occupied philosophers for millennia, yet we rarely begin our thinking about technology with it. Instead, we ask whether a new tool works, whether it is efficient, whether it solves a problem we recognize. We evaluate technologies on their own terms—and in doing so, we often fail to ask whether the terms themselves have been changed by the tools we use.

This is the deeper challenge technology poses to human flourishing: not merely that our devices might distract us or displace human connection, but that they may be reshaping the very conditions upon which a good life depends. The question is not simply whether technology serves our vision of flourishing, but whether that vision is being quietly redrawn by the instruments we employ. To think seriously about technology and human flourishing, we must begin by asking what flourishing actually requires—and then examine whether the direction of technological change takes us toward or away from it.

Most substantive accounts of human flourishing share a surprising feature: they involve struggle. Not suffering for its own sake, but the experience of overcoming resistance—of working through difficulty to arrive at something meaningful. The athlete who trains through pain and exhaustion and crosses a finish line understands this; so does the musician who spends years mastering an instrument, the scholar who struggles through a difficult text, the parent who sacrifices sleep for a child. Flourishing, on these accounts, is not a state of passive satisfaction but an activity, a process of working toward and achieving things that matter—and doing so against some form of resistance.

This observation is not merely philosophical speculation. It describes something we recognize in our own experience: the satisfaction of a job well done, the depth of a relationship forged through shared hardship, the solidity of a character built through facing adversity. The psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi's concept of "flow"—the state of complete absorption in a challenging task—captures something similar: deep satisfaction arises when we are stretched to the limits of our capacities and meet the challenge.

What happens, then, when technology systematically removes friction from life? This is the question that should concern us most, because it goes beyond the familiar anxieties about attention spans and social comparison. The technological trajectory is not merely toward distraction but toward the elimination of difficulty itself. We can order food without cooking, travel without walking, find answers without remembering, connect without risk of rejection. Each convenience is small; the cumulative effect may be profound.

Consider the phenomenon of algorithmic recommendation. Netflix suggests what to watch; Spotify selects the next song; Amazon proposes what to buy. On the surface, this seems obviously good—why waste time on mediocrity when excellence is available on demand? But the friction of choosing, of sometimes choosing poorly, of discovering something unexpected through the act of searching, is not merely an inefficiency to be eliminated. It is the process by which we discover what we actually value. When algorithms do the selecting, we may end up with more satisfaction in the narrow sense of immediate pleasure while losing the deeper satisfaction of having shaped our own preferences through effortful choice.

This is the paradox at the heart of technology and flourishing: the things we typically want from technology are the very things that may undermine the conditions for a flourishing life. We want efficiency, convenience, frictionless experience. But friction is not merely an obstacle to flourishing—it is often the substance through which flourishing is achieved.

This does not mean technology is inherently harmful to flourishing. That position is neither true nor helpful. Technology has always been a means by which human beings extend their capabilities, solve problems, and reduce suffering. The medical technologies that have eradicated diseases and extended life expectancy are unambiguous goods; the same is true of technologies that restore hearing, sight, and mobility to those who lacked them. To dismiss these innovations as irrelevant to flourishing would be to define human flourishing so narrowly that it becomes almost contemptible.

Nor is it accurate to say that previous generations' anxieties about new technologies have always been proven wrong. The printing press was indeed accused of spreading dangerous ideas, but it also democratized knowledge and enabled the Enlightenment. The telegraph was indeed blamed for destroying the art of letter-writing, and in a sense it did—but it also allowed families separated by migration to maintain connection in ways previously impossible. Each technology brings genuine benefits and genuine costs, and the record of past anxieties does not tell us how to weigh the present.

What the historical record does suggest, however, is that we consistently underestimate the costs while overestimating the benefits—or rather, we evaluate new technologies in terms of what they add while failing to anticipate what they displace. We拥抱 the smartphone for its convenience without fully reckoning with what it might be crowding out: the capacity for sustained attention, for boredom, for the kind of idle contemplation that historically preceded deep insight. We celebrate the connectivity of social media while overlooking the way it might be replacing the deeper forms of belonging that human beings have always needed.

The question of artificial intelligence intensifies these concerns dramatically. For most of human history, the things that made us distinctively human—our creativity, our judgment, our capacity for wisdom in practical matters—seemed beyond the reach of mechanical replication. If AI can now compose music that moves us, write prose that persuades us, and diagnose illness more accurately than human doctors, what remains as the distinctive ground of human flourishing?

This is not primarily a question about employment, though the economic disruptions of automation are real and demand serious policy responses. It is a question about meaning. Work has historically provided not just income but structure, purpose, and the experience of contributing to something larger than oneself. If machines can perform most productive labor, we will need not merely economic planning but a cultural and philosophical reimagining of what makes life meaningful. The challenge is not that people will be idle but that they will lack the forms of engagement through which human beings have historically found their lives worthwhile.

More subtly, we should consider what happens to human creative expression when machines can produce competent art. Not that human art will cease to exist—people will always want to create—but that the meaning of human creativity may shift. If anyone can generate a passable poem or melody with the right prompt, what does it mean for a human being to compose one? Perhaps it means something deeper: not the production of a artifact but the process of working through difficulty, of developing a craft through years of practice, of expressing something that could only come from a particular human life lived in a particular way. Or perhaps the ground shifts beneath our feet entirely, and we find that meaning was always tied to capacities we thought were permanent but were in fact contingent.

I do not know the answer to this question, and I suspect no one does. What I am confident about is that we should approach these possibilities with more humility than either the techno-optimists or the skeptics typically display. The optimists are right that technology has repeatedly transformed life for the better in ways that early critics did not anticipate. They are wrong if they believe this pattern will continue automatically, without careful attention to what we might be losing. The skeptics are right that the costs of technology are often invisible until they have accumulated. They are wrong if they believe the answer is to reject technology entirely—that is neither possible nor desirable.

What we need, perhaps, is a different kind of thinking altogether. Not optimism or pessimism, but a stubborn attention to what actually constitutes flourishing—and a willingness to forgo some capabilities even when they are available. There is something to the old idea of voluntary poverty, of deliberately living with less in order to preserve space for what matters. Perhaps we need something similar with technology: not abstinence, but a principled refusal to adopt every capability that becomes available.

This is uncomfortable. It goes against the grain of a technological culture that measures progress in capabilities acquired. But if flourishing requires struggle, if it requires friction and difficulty and the satisfaction of overcoming resistance, then the unexamined pursuit of technological capability may be moving us in precisely the wrong direction. The question is not whether we can do more with our tools, but whether the things we can do still constitute a life worth living.

I do not offer this as a conclusion. It is, rather, a question that I believe we should carry with us as we navigate an age of unprecedented technological power: What kind of life do we want to live, and what role should our extraordinary capabilities play in it? The answer will not be simple, and it will not be the same for everyone. But the asking itself may be the most important thing we do.
